item.title: Good tools are invisible
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Good tools are invisible

Ginger Bill

9 minutes by Ginger Bill Good tools should be invisible. When a tool starts creating friction, that's a flaw, not a feature. Yet many people reframe their tools' weaknesses as fun puzzles to solve, then mistake that feeling of cleverness for real productivity. The best sign a tool is working for you is that you stop noticing it entirely. Implementing Production Agent Memory Without Distributed
item.description: Good tools are invisible

item.title: Broker-visible vs client-local parallelism
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Broker-visible vs client-local parallelism

Jack Vanlightly

4 minutes by Jack Vanlightly Share groups in Kafka are designed to add queue-like behavior to a log, not primarily to parallelize work. To figure out how much parallelism you need, Jack suggests multiplying your message rate by average processing time. If each unit of parallelism maps to a broker-managed consumer, costs grow fast. Keeping parallelism on the client side through virtual threads or async tasks is cheaper and requires far fewer connections.
item.description: Broker-visible vs client-local parallelism

item.title: How Claude code works, from tokens to agents
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Claude code works, from tokens to agents

Nemanja Stojanovic

28 minutes by Nemanja Stojanovic Tools like Claude Code, ChatGPT, and Cursor look like magic from the outside. You type a message, and the AI reads your files, fixes bugs, runs tests. Under the hood, it’s a stack of pieces, and once you see them, the behavior of these tools gets a lot more predictable. Nemanja's walkthrough builds that stack from scratch, starting from the simplest possible interaction and adding layers until we arrive at something like Claude Code.
item.description: How Claude code works, from tokens to agents

item.title: Work loudly
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Work loudly

Ben Balter

6 minutes by Ben Balter Remote work removes the ambient visibility that offices provide for free. To compensate, share work as it happens rather than summarizing it afterward: open issues before you have answers, write pull request descriptions that explain your thinking, and post blockers in public channels. This creates a searchable trail that helps managers advocate for you, lets teammates contribute early, and ensures decisions reach stakeholders before they become surprises.
item.description: Work loudly

item.title: Building service topology at scale
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building service topology at scale

Parth Jain et al.

24 minutes by Parth Jain et al. How Netflix built a real-time service topology system to map connections between services at a very large scale. They describe the system's architecture, the challenges faced in production, and the solutions used to improve performance, reliability, and scalability. The lessons learned show how careful design, continuous testing, and optimization help build efficient distributed systems. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Building service topology at scale

item.title: Cache stampede: When our cache turned against us
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Cache stampede: When our cache turned against us

Bart Wullems

Cache stampedes happen when many requests all miss the cache at the same moment and hit the database together. A simple fix is adding a per-key lock using SemaphoreSlim, so only one request rebuilds the cache while others wait and reuse the result. ASP.NET Core's built-in HybridCache handles this automatically. Adding random jitter to expiry times also helps prevent many keys from expiring all at once.
item.description: Cache stampede: When our cache turned against us

item.title: Role-based authorization in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Role-based authorization in ASP.NET Core

Mukesh Murugan

Roles in JWTs are just claims with an agreed name. Mukesh suggests to write role claims at login, set RoleClaimType to match, then protect endpoints with RequireRole or the Authorize attribute. A common silent bug occurs when claim mapping renames your role claim to a long URI, causing every role check to return 403 with no error. Multiple roles in one call mean OR, while chained calls mean AND, and repeated checks belong in a named policy.
item.description: Role-based authorization in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Redesigning the NServiceBus pipeline yet again
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Redesigning the NServiceBus pipeline yet again

David Boike, Daniel Marbach

The NServiceBus message pipeline was redesigned to support modern .NET trimming and ahead-of-time compilation, which ban the dynamic code generation the old approach relied on. The solution uses default interface members to build a statically typed chain where each behavior wires directly to the next at startup. The result is a pipeline that starts 330 times faster, runs 25 to 29% faster on the success path, and existing custom behaviors require no changes to benefit.
item.description: Redesigning the NServiceBus pipeline yet again

item.title: ASP.NET Core background tasks with NCronJob and SignalR
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
ASP.NET Core background tasks with NCronJob and SignalR

Damien Bod

NCronJob is an open source NuGet package for running background jobs in ASP.NET Core. It works by implementing a simple IJob interface and supports both concurrent and non-concurrent job execution. In this demo Damien uses it to send messages every five seconds through SignalR, displaying them in a Razor Pages UI.
item.description: ASP.NET Core background tasks with NCronJob and SignalR

item.title: Discriminated unions in C# and .NET 11 (for real this time)
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Discriminated unions in C# and .NET 11 (for real this time)

Maarten Balliauw

C# 15 adds native union types, letting you declare that a value is exactly one of several types in a single line. The compiler handles implicit conversions and, most usefully, enforces exhaustive pattern matching, so missing a case in a switch expression raises a warning. This removes the need for workarounds like the OneOf package or hand-rolled implicit operators. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Discriminated unions in C# and .NET 11 (for real this time)

0;"><span>The OpenTelemetry Collector receives this data from all services in a unified format.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The collector splits the data into three streams: traces, logs, and metrics.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each stream is sent to a Receive & Process unit that prepares it for storage and analysis.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Processed data is stored in a Log Database for querying and long-term access.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Data from the database is visualized through a Visualization dashboard for monitoring and debugging.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over to you: What else will you add to better understand distributed tracing?</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Life of a Redis Query</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Redis is an in-memory database, which means all data lives in RAM for speed. However, if the server crashes or restarts, data could be lost. </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To solve this problem, Redis provides two persistence mechanisms to write data to disk:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AOF (Append-Only File)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a client sends a command, Redis first executes it in memory (RAM). After that, Redis logs the command by appending it to an AOF file on disk. This ensures every operation can be replayed later to rebuild the dataset. Since the command is executed first and logged afterward, writes are non-blocking. The recovery process uses the event log to replay the recorded commands.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>RDB (Redis Database)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead of writing every command, Redis can periodically take snapshots of the entire dataset.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main thread forks a subprocess (bgsave) that shares all the in-memory data of the main thread. The bgsave subprocess reads the data from the main thread and writes it to the RDB file.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Redis uses copy-on-write. When the main thread modifies data, a copy of the data is created, and the process works on that so that writes don’t get blocked. The snapshot is then written as an RDB file on disk, allowing Redis to quickly reload the snapshot into memory when needed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mixed Approach</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In production, Redis often uses both AOF and RDB. RDB provides fast reloads with compact snapshots. AOF guarantees durability by recording every operation since the last snapshot.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Over to you: Have you used Redis in your project?</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: item.title: How Do I Deal With My Team Members Who Are Resisting Change?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Do I Deal With My Team Members Who Are Resisting Change?

Andi Roberts

“Every leader eventually meets the same person. Arms folded in the meeting. The one who says “we tried this before” before you have finished the sentence. The one whose email replies get a little shorter each time the project is mentioned. It is tempting to label this person difficult, negative, or stuck. It is also, usually, the wrong diagnosis.”

#Management ConflictResolution

item.title: Code Yellow, Code Red
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Code Yellow, Code Red

James Stanier

Here’s what we’re going to cover: (1) What Code Yellow and Code Red actually mean, and where the terms come from. (2) How we ran ours at Provet: the structure, the work, and what we learned. (3) A generalised template you can adapt for your own organisation. (4) When to call one, when to escalate, and the failure modes to watch for.

#Management Incidents CaseStudy
item.description: Code Yellow, Code Red

item.title: What Does “Playing Politics" Mean For Software Engineers?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
What Does “Playing Politics" Mean For Software Engineers?

Sean Goedecke

“Playing politics isn’t about plotting and scheming, and it isn’t just about being a friendly, likeable person (although that helps). It’s about figuring out how your company actually operates: who makes the decisions, who gets consulted, what behavior gets rewarded, and so on. The most basic way to do that is to figure out who is powerful, get out of their way, and (if you can) help them get what they want.”

#CareerGrowth Influence
item.description: What Does “Playing Politics" Mean For Software Engineers?

item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Benford's Law: The Strange Law That Catches Financial Fraudsters

Vatsal Bakshi

In almost any large dataset drawn from the real world — populations of cities, lengths of rivers, prices, earthquake depths, company revenues — the leading digit is not uniformly distributed. The digit 1 appears as the first digit about 30% of the time. Not 11%. Nearly three times the naive expectation. The digit 9 appears less than 5% of the time.

#Security Algo
item.description: Benford's Law: The Strange Law That Catches Financial Fraudsters

item.title: Quadrupling Code Performance With A “Useless" If
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Quadrupling Code Performance With A “Useless" If

Alisa Sireneva

“We don’t expect too many chunks, so next_j[i][j] is quite likely to just be equal to j. If we could tell the CPU to predict that j stays intact, the loop would become throughput-bound rather than latency-bound.”

#Debugging Performance DeepDive

style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups. Notice an interesting event or trend? Hit reply and share it with me.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Grok’s CLI uploaded all your local files to the cloud, then got caught</span></strong><span>. Just as devs were starting to use the Grok CLI – thanks to the capable Grok 4.5 coding model – they discover that all local files, .env files and git history have been pushed to a GCP bucket, unencrypted. SpaceX’s initial reaction was to blame devs for not opting out of something engineers had no idea they were opted into.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>New trend: concern about massive increase in code review load. </span></strong><span>Top of mind for engineering leaders: what to do about the ever-growing code review load, and how devs are starting to review code less thoroughly than before? Many questions, but few proven solutions. </span><em><span>Send comments about what you see working.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Are more devs at enterprises upset about enterprise pricing by AI labs – and does it matter? </span></strong><span>I got a message from a reader baffled to learn their company pays 20-30x the price for tokens than their own $20/month Claude Code / Codex subscription. It may show how valuable AI coding tools are.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Linux creator: AI “clearly useful.” </span></strong><span>Inside the Linux kernel maintainers group, the discussion veered onto whether Linux should consider banning AI contributions, similar to how some FOSS projects have done so. Linus Torvalds weighed in and made it clear that AI is useful, everyone should decide whether to use it, but no one is allowed to tell others what tools to use. Given AI is an increasingly capable tool, it would be foolish to not use it as such.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Grok’s CLI uploaded all your local files to the cloud, then got caught</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Last week, xAI (Elon Musk’s AI company, now part of SpaceX) released the Grok 4.5 model, built by Cursor (an acquisition), trained on SpaceX GPUs, and branded “Grok.” It’s a pretty good model; benchmarking as close in coding capability to Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.5 – while being 60-70% lower cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Grok 4.5 can be used via API, but is easiest used via the Grok Build coding CLI. So, that’s what many devs did. Some of them have noticed something </span><em><span>really</span></em><span> weird: the CLI is uploading all their local files in their working directories! Here’s an independent AI safety researcher known as ‘Cerblab’ </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4538d74-b970-493f-82d9-6839f5d4f1d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>documenting what is happening</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“xAI’s official Grok Build coding CLI (grok), on a normal consumer login, does three things worth documenting precisely:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>It transmits the contents of files it reads — including a .env secrets file — to xAI, verbatim and unredacted</span></strong><span>. The secret appears in two channels: the live model turn (POST /v1/responses) and a session_state archive uploaded and accepted (HTTP 200) via POST /v1/storage — the endpoint the binary routes to the grok-code-session-traces GCS bucket (see section 5).</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>It uploads the whole repository — every tracked file’s content plus git history — independent of what the agent reads. </span></strong><span>Grok packages the workspace and uploads it via POST /v1/storage. Proven directly: on a real codebase, with the prompt “reply OK, do not read any files”, Grok uploaded the entire repo as a git bundle (POST /v1/storage → 200); git cloning the captured bundle recovers a file the agent was told not to open — src/_probe/never_read_canary.txt — with its unique marker verbatim, plus the full git history (appendix uploaded_repo.bundle). And it scales: on a 12 GB repo of never-read random files, /v1/storage moved 5.10 GiB, all HTTP 200 (truncated mid-stream), while the model-turn channel moved just 192 KB — a ~27,800× ratio that pins the upload to the codebase, not to what was read. No storage upload failed; the only non-200s were a model-usage quota (402/429) on /v1/responses and one unrelated 404 — not a storage size cap.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>The storage destination is a Google Cloud Storage bucket, grok-code-session-traces</span></strong><span> (not AWS S3) — named verbatim in the binary and in a captured metadata.json (gs://grok-code-session-traces/…). I did not find this mechanism surfaced in the CLI’s install/quickstart materials (not an exhaustive docs audit — §7), it is active by default, and disabling “Improve the model” does not turn it off (/v1/settings still returned trace_upload_enabled: true; §6).</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>None of this proves xAI trains on the data — that is a policy question addressed in [section] 6. What is proven is transmission, acceptance, and storage.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s so much wrong with this approach! To name a few:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sending your codebase over the context window is not normal. </span></strong><span>All AI agents send over their context window to the server that runs the LLM. That’s where tokenization happens and the context is appended to the session. This means that other AI agents send over some part of the code that they read in their context window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No need to send over the source code to index it. </span></strong><span>Indexing the codebase is important for efficient code lookup, and we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/63defea0-3885-4e96-a384-db816c09773f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered how Cursor does this in a privacy-conscious way</span></a><span> by indexing a user’s codebase locally, creating embeddings, and sending those embeddings to the server. Cursor’s server does not store any of the user’s codebase though. Except that Grok CLI transferred all users’ codebases to a cloud bucket! </span><em><span>Given Cursor and Grok are now combined as part of SpaceX, it’s a real head scratcher why the Grok CLI isn’t doing what Cursor always has.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sending over unencrypted .env files is reckless. </span></strong><span>Local .env files store secrets, database access tokens, service access tokens, and more. These are sensitive pieces of information that need to be handled with care. If transmitted, they should be encrypted at the very least. Grok / SpaceX storing them on the GCP storage bucket – likely unencrypted – is flat-out unacceptable and reason enough for any sensible company to ban usage of Grok CLI.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No good reason to upload git history. </span></strong><span>Sure, seeing Git history could be helpful when training an AI model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>It’s malicious to not tell devs anything about it. </span></strong><span>Developers using Grok CLI haven’t been asked to opt into this data upload, nor notified of it. Most evidently had no idea this has been happening, and are understandably furious after Cerblab’s writeup went viral.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>SpaceX throws devs “under the bus”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Caught red-handed, Grok CLI disabled file uploads with a remote feature flag. </span></strong><span>AWS engineer Wes Eklund started tracking upload functionality with the CLI, finding that the uploads suddenly stopped due to a feature flag being flipped by the Grok team, pausing data collection.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the code functionality to stream all local files to the server, unencrypted, remained present in the CLI, even in later updates. Read an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dae033e3-414f-4836-80cb-8a580c9aa109?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in-depth analysis by Wes.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>SpaceX’s official response was pretty laughable, </span></strong><span>not explaining why .env files and .git history were uploaded, and adding that enterprise customers with zero data retention (ZDR) enabled were the only ones unaffected by underhanded, secret uploading of users’ local files:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Translation: “Enterprise users with ZDR turned on were not impacted. To everyone else: we didn’t tell you about this hidden/privacy command, but it’s your fault. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf8f5a9b-08e2-44b0-97d5-75492b10d097?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>SpaceX</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My initial reaction is what a condescending response by SpaceX, swiftly followed by the question: does Grok CLI even have enterprise customers? It might be few, given how reckless the team evidently is by uploading unencrypted secrets! SpaceX CEO Elon Musk chimed in with a post that seemed to be almost trolling angry users. He </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7bfcad87-a7aa-46b3-bf92-bdee8cae9d48?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wrote</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“SpaceX policy regarding data retention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is actually helpful for debugging issues if we can retain some amount of data, so allowing this would be appreciated, but your privacy settings are always respected.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This makes it worse because SpaceX has been secretly uploading far more data than is “useful for debugging!” Uploading the git history and sensitive .env files is </span><em><span>not</span></em><span>, in any way, useful for debugging. Also, Grok/SpaceX did not upload “some amount of data”; it uploaded every last file it could find in your local folder.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The developer community is justifiably upset to read SpaceX and Musk pretending that Grok has only uploaded scraps of data purely for debugging purposes. This time, even fans of SpaceX and Grok are speaking out against Musk and his company’s behavior. AWS engineer </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8cc3aa41-1e2e-46f6-a2b4-f9f45ce8c1a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Wes Eklund</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Elon, firstly, huge fan of everything you work on. Completely understand the need for some trace data to improve customer experiences.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From what I’ve researched, it seems to be much more than just trace debugging issues. It seems to be entire code repos with sensitive information just collected entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Your Google Cloud blob storage must have petabytes of code repos from us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not ideal.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Sam Altman pushes Grok to open source Grok CLI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, also posted, using a term Musk often employs when commenting on things he disapproves of in society, and hinting at the benefits of Codex which doesn’t upload your whole local filesystem, or mess with .env files and the git history. Altman’s comment seemingly hit home. Also, SpaceX has stated it is deleting data from its servers, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcd82be7-0f67-431c-aa4d-6a1bfbdf1aaa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>writing</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We disabled default retention for all Grok Build users starting on July 12th. Additionally, we are deleting all coding data that was previously retained, ensuring every user’s preferences are respected. With these steps, Grok Build goes beyond other major coding products to protect user privacy.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The open sourced repo is rushed, unsurprisingly.</span></strong><span> Kernel engineer Elliot Arledge used the repo and reported what he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59ba8357-01ea-4a64-a04b-6432200eef9b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>found</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Out of the box, `cargo test --workspace` doesn’t compile. 190+ errors, all one bug class: cross-crate test helpers hidden behind #[cfg(test)], which Bazel’s per-target test builds tolerate but Cargo doesn’t, because a dependency is never compiled in test mode. The default-bazel feature is declared in ~20 manifests and wired to nothing. Ungating the benign helpers and putting the signing-key test seam behind a dev-dependency-only feature gets the suite running for the first time on the published tree: 24,663 passed, 28 failed, and every one of the 28 is a pre-existing bug the broken build had been hiding (tests reading your real ~/.claude/settings.json, a tool missing from the registry, macOS /var symlink breakage, one Theme::current() race).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Questions for the team:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Did anyone try downloading this repo and running it before publishing?”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In fairness, it’s clear from the outside that the dev team was instructed to open source the repo ASAP, and did just that. I would expect improvements to allow the developer community to compile the repo and run tests will come later.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a side note, I wonder what the mood within Grok is. A mandate to open source the product – that was not built to be open sourced! – and doing it in a couple of hours hints what it’s like to work there. Some folks doubtless would find it thrilling and a big challenge, while others likely find it pretty stressful having the “Eye of Sauron” (the CEO) upon them!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Can companies trust Grok now?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To hand it to Grok/SpaceX, the last 24 hours of this incident saw some impressive execution. In contrast, everything that took place beforehand screams “amateur hour”:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did no one in teams that wrote the functionality to upload the complete local codebase raise concerns that this would be unacceptable to devs?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How did uploading secrets without encryption not raise alarm bells?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why greenlight any of it without opt-in and do it in a secretive manner?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For sensible companies generating revenue with software, vendors who are allowed to access their codebase are limited to those that can be trusted. Grok has demonstrated it is unprepared to handle codebases with security fundamentals in mind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s now frantic backpedaling and rapid open sourcing, but my impression is that this is simply because Grok/SpaceX was caught red-handed, and understands the risk of losing enterprise contracts caused by this flagrant breach of trust. This is why SpaceX’s communication mentioned that enterprise customers with zero data retention have not been impacted!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Trust is earned in drops and lost in buckets; SpaceX/Grok will likely learn this. </span></strong><span>By secretly uploading codebases and secrets, Grok CLI revealed itself as an untrustworthy coding agent that’s a risk to use. Meanwhile, all the major competitors – Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI – have never violated user trust this way.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Grok CLI can rebuild trust, but it’ll likely take years of no security-related incidents to prove they are an open source-first product (that they were not, just a day ago!), and also demonstrate that they care about “normal” developers, and not just enterprise clients with ZDR turned on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This incident is a good reminder of why planning and process can slow shipping speed, but increase revenue generation. </span></strong><span>I would wager that the Grok team has shrunk SpaceX’s enterprise subscription prospects for the foreseeable, in the name of saving a few hours on security reviews, learning what other coding harnesses do with codebase uploads, or even just asking the Cursor team!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I predict Grok/SpaceX will have to offer very high usage limits inside the Grok CLI to convince devs to take a risk on running this software on their system. And they will have to undercut OpenAI and Anthropic API pricing massively for any security team to greenlight use of a CLI that just last week was sending .env secrets unencrypted to their GCP buckets.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, SpaceX/Grok will be just fine as it has the capital to fix things. It will now just be a lot more expensive and time-consuming to fix something that was likely caused by a few engineers wanting to make debugging easier!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. New trend: concern about massive increase in code review load</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing I am hearing that’s top of mind for many engineering leaders is what is being done to deal with the continuous increase in code review load. It’s been a topic for a while, and more such conversations seem to be taking place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For me, it began in January, when Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.4 started to write more and better code at most companies. Around then, Director-level folks started talking about the bottleneck of building software moving from coding to the review phase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>There’s been a boom in AI code review tools to deal with the increase in load since February</span></strong><span>, and an explosion of experimentation with and adoption of dedicated AI code review tools like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/734dfb99-5af7-4877-a44b-1a72dc1dd9da?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>CodeRabbit</span></a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbd6c099-ccab-463c-a231-dc7495680e0b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Greptile</span></a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/382f8a6a-56f2-433f-9a1c-c47fe9e2d6a2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Qodo</span></a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c169d9f-3a63-46be-97ad-319aadad54b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>SonarQube</span></a><span> (now also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/68309f12-7162-496a-a253-0dd52474c6b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Gitar</span></a><span>). There’s also tools offered by coding harnesses themselves like Claude Code review, Cursor review, GitHub Copilot review. And then tools previously not involved in code reviews – but which have context on the codebase – are also adding this, like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3e4a2e22-eaaa-4e43-86b4-9298d5142cb9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Sentry’s Seer AI reviews</span></a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/245b766a-6193-416c-9487-6a9a5135c86e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Linear code reviews</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Larger companies are building href="https://substack.com/redirect/7699846d-901b-4223-8f9c-4dd1bd3143d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>how Uber uses AI for software development</span></a><span>, and it’s not just Uber: companies like Cloudflare (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f9943844-ea19-4952-befd-af371d18bc6c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>AI Code Reviewer</span></a><span>), Faire (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/996be387-4660-431d-b0bb-27e43a9367fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Fairey</span></a><span>), and HubSpot (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0608a71e-eee6-407f-912f-cfb08c17a0c4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Sidekick</span></a><span>) and many others have also built tools to make their code review flows more fluid, after finding that an in-house implementation worked better than integrating a vendor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Another approach is thinking about how to verify code, instead of reviewing.</span></strong><span> This is easier said than done; in theory, thorough testing should be able to verify that code works as expected. But how much testing is ‘thorough’? What type of tests are we talking about? Integration and end-to-end as well? What about fuzz testing? Or formal methods? What about verifying that new tests exercise the functionality as expected? And how do we connect all of this with observability?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Too much thorough code review is burning out engineers, and resulting in sub-par code reviews. </span></strong><span>I hear a lot anecdotally that devs see others as no longer able to review code with intent, whereby, if the AI code review has no real comments, they just approve it. Meanwhile, those devs who put the same effort and energy into code review as before feel overloaded by AI slop PRs sent their way.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problems exist, and the solutions feel more like experiments.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What are you seeing inside your company, and how are you dealing with the increase in code reviews? Share your ideas for practical, workable “replacements”?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Are more devs inside enterprises starting to get upset at enterprise pricing by the AI labs? And does it matter if so?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A long-time reader got in touch, who’s a software engineer:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>“I think it’s crazy that OpenAI and Anthropic are charging enterprise customers roughly 20-30x on inference than they do people who are using subs. I did some open source work over the weekend on my Claude Code and Codex subscriptions, using 5% of weekly rate limits. I calculated how much the same would have cost using API pricing: and it was ~$450!! On my personal subscription, this was a $20 cost.</span><br><br><span>I am starting to feel like these AI labs are just flaunting that in the face of enterprise customers when they talk about all these generous rate limits and resets. Enterprise gets no such reprieve when they have issues.</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I sense that these AI labs are really starting to piss off a lot of enterprise customers.</span></strong><span> I imagine the subscriptions are heavily subsidized and will go away once the IPOs happen, but the difference in billing is jaw-dropping.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s known that Claude Code and Codex’s personal subscriptions are heavily “subsidized” compared to API pricing. A 10-30x difference in cost is what I’ve heard it adds up to.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On one hand, this is pretty clearly  the go-to market strategy for these companies: lure in devs and small companies to use Claude Code and Codex with these very generous limits on the $20/$100/$200/month plan. But once a company with 100+ devs adopts the tools, charge them 20x or so more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon Willison called this OpenAI and Anthropic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/743c5261-1116-41cb-bd26-1b65dae2a7fa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>finding their product-market fits</span></a><span>. AI labs can get away charging so much to companies that make a lot of money from software because these tools either help them make more money or they save money. Being able to sell tokens at a profit to large companies helps AI labs to build large businesses that could IPO in the future.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, yes, I can understand being taken aback by how expensive tokens are for enterprises, but if they’re not footing the bill, will devs care? I talked with a Head of Engineering who is spending $40-50K/month on Fable, while their company is generating $3M/employee in revenue, and is profitable. They said they are fine with paying enterprise API prices for tokens if it  means they can ship products faster and can hire slower, and serve more customers.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Linux creator: AI “clearly useful”</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Linux creator and top-level maintainer Linus Torvalds </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2887c196-d264-43e0-a5c1-b40ac701e690?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared his opinion</span></a><span> on using AI for development in the Linux kernel. This response comes after some mainatiners urged Linux to consider a zero-tolerance approach to any LLM-generated contriubitions, similar to how some free and open source (FOSS) projects </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b24d0e69-3369-4ef9-a213-6a012bae5e47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>have done so</span></a><span>. Linus’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2887c196-d264-43e0-a5c1-b40ac701e690?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reply</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I realize that some people really dislike AI, but this is an area where I’m willing to absolutely put my foot down as the top-level maintainer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects, and if somebody has issues with that, they can do the open-source thing and fork it. Or just walk away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI is a tool, just like other tools we use.  And it’s clearly a useful one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>[AI] may not have been that “clearly [useful]” even just a year ago, but it’s no longer in question today.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are other questions around AI (like what the economy of it will actually look like in the end), but “is it useful” is no longer one of those questions. Anybody who doubts that clearly hasn’t actually used it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yes, it can also be a somewhat painful tool, both for maintainer workloads and just from a “it keeps finding embarrassing bugs” standpoint.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the solution is not to put your head in the sand and sing “La La La, I can’t hear you” at the top of your voice like some people seem to do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The solution is to make sure those LLM tools </span><em><span>help</span></em><span> maintainers instead of just causing them pain. There’s no question on that side.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re not forcing anybody to use it, but I will very loudly ignore people who try to argue against other people from using it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And no, AI isn’t perfect. But Christ, anybody who points to the problems at AI had better be looking in the mirror and pointing at themselves at the same time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because it’s not like natural intelligence is always all that great either.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The kernel project has been and will continue to be about the technology.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sure, the social angle of working on open source is important and often a very motivating part of the project, but in the end that’s a side benefit, not the _point_ of the project.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is NOT some kind of “social warrior” project, never has been, and never will be.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the kernel community we do open source because it results in better technology, not because of religious reasons.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And so we make decisions primarily based on technical merit. Not fear of new tools.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For coding and software development in general, AI has proven useful, hence why pretty much the whole industry has adopted AI coding tools, and more AI-powered tools are spreading across the development lifecycle, from AI code reviews to help with observability, incident management, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/68395d2a-b0c7-4c94-a4cd-50f976b0c42f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the same thread</span></a><span>, Linux attempts to persuade a contributor to try AI tools before making up their mind about it:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“No, AI reports are not always great, but neither are human reviews. I see less useful reviews by humans where I go “did this person just try to get his name in the commit log, because that has no useful content”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I suspect you haven’t used AI for programming. Try it. Try one of the </span><em><span>good</span></em><span> ones.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I don’t mean “use it for the kernel”. Use it just for the fun of it. Find something you want to do, and just play with it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The open models are getting pretty darn good too, but for a first trial without any real setup, one of the free tiers of the cloud ones is certainly the easiest way to just kick the tires.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Do it with something you find interesting, but not “important” - start small, and start with something you feel you probably wouldn’t really waste your time on if it was just yourself, but where you have enough background knowledge that you can judge the output.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s what I did [play around with AI], because I wanted to judge things based on real use, not on what others say</span></strong><span> (and sometimes the loudest ones do it for marketing reasons because they have stock that is tied to it).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You might find it enlightening, or at least interesting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My own personal annoyance was how eager to please AI models tend to be at least by default. I understand why it happens, and that people like that subservient tone, but at least personally I was looking for a more critical review of the code, not an AI that had been taught to say “You are entirely right” just to please people.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>The conversation ended with Linus </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5cac31fb-8af9-4264-a66c-c9909892b593?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stating</span></a><span> that kernel developers are free to choose their tools and whether to use AI. This is a grounded take, and I especially agree that us professionals should avoid making decisions on AI tools based on heresay: just try them, see where they help, and where they fall short. And once it’s part of the day-to-day work, figure out where they create new problems – like now, with code review. 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Every software company that builds an application serving more than one customer has to answer this question.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Should each customer get a separate copy of the system, or should they all share one?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Running a dedicated copy per customer is easy to reason about, but the cost of maintaining hundreds of separate copies increases with every new customer. On the other hand, sharing a single system across all customers is far cheaper. This is why most of the software we use every day is built to be shared rather than duplicated. Such systems are known as multi-tenant systems, where each customer is a tenant that shares resources with other tenants.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, sharing is also where the difficulty begins.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once many customers rely on the same database, the same servers, and the same background jobs, their fortunes become linked. For example, one customer running a heavy report can slow the service for everyone alongside them. A single faulty deployment can impact all of them at once instead of just the customer. And the most serious risk is around data leaks, where one customer is shown data that belongs to another. All of these situations have to be actively handled by a multi-tenant system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will understand multi-tenant architecture from the basics, along with its various benefits and challenges.
