Buildkite was stress-tested at the largest scale inside companies solving some of the hardest engineering problems. It’s built to reliably manage whatever your coding agents throw at the build queue, today, next year and beyond. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ae643820-bf3b-49f3-a72c-482a0c18613b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Learn more.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c1b2716-3d14-4c94-8076-1b601336d9c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Sentry</span></a></strong><span> – application monitoring software built by developers, for developers. Sentry’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f8da4de4-2e0c-433a-8d95-58700b1a8080?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Seer AI agent</span></a><span> is one of their new, neat tools, as a way to debug errors faster. Same with Sentry’s MCP server. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c1b2716-3d14-4c94-8076-1b601336d9c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Check out Sentry</span></a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowing how LLM contexts work and how to work around context limitations – aka “context engineering” – is becoming more important for software engineers working with LLMs. Let’s look into what works and what doesn’t, today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, I sit down with the CEO and cofounder of HumanLayer, Dex Horthy, who coined the term “context engineering”. We discuss the ideas behind this context engineering, harness engineering, loop engineering, software factories, why his approach to AI-assisted software development has evolved, and how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da35a3fc-1c61-4355-8718-54782b54c98e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>HumanLayer</span></a><span> is helping engineering teams automate more of the software development lifecycle without sacrificing code quality.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Key observations from Dex</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here are 12 useful points Dex made in our conversation:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c3d06ce8-88a4-4a74-bbe9-ca9075bd6035?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/Usufn8IQJgw" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Dex talked with ~100 “real” AI Engineers and wrote the popular ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e291d757-9977-434a-aa78-f660baddaf63?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>12-Factor Agents - Principles for building reliable LLM applications</span></a></strong><span>’ based on what he learned. Around August 2024, he started to build AI agents when the common approach was to use frameworks like LangChain and CrewAI, and also talked with around 100 AI engineers doing tangible work such as taking on $100K+ contracts to ship AI solutions within enterprises. They tried those frameworks and discarded them in favor of building their own pipelines. Dex shared the learnings from the conversations in his hit book, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e291d757-9977-434a-aa78-f660baddaf63?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>12-Factor Agents</span></a><span>. </span><em><span>It’s a great read!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Lesson learned: Shipping unread code spells disaster within months. </span></strong><span>Dex experimented with having the model write the code and humans not reviewing anything in July 2025. Four months later, they shut things down and threw the whole system out. Production broke, and no matter how much the team prompted Opus 4.1, the model could not find the root cause.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It took days of wading through spaghetti code to discover the primary key wrongly routed through the complete codebase. Once fixed, it took three weeks to re-onboard to a codebase no human had ever read. Today, Dex thinks this problem wouldn’t even take four months to develop, now that newer models produce code a </span><em><span>lot</span></em><span> faster than a year ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Today’s coding models are most likely trained in a way that makes codebases </span></strong><em><strong><span>worse</span></strong></em><strong><span> over time. </span></strong><span>Dex believes that the reason we see LLMs “degrade” existing codebases is because they are optimized to do well on SWE-bench-style benchmarks. These benchmarks reward reproducing a known fix in codebases like Django, but cannot measure poor architecture decisions. This is because the cost function of bad architecture and bad program design cannot be evaluated by running a unit test.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>It’s a tricky problem to solve: Dex’s best guess is an eval of a model building 20 features in a row in a codebase without knowing what’s coming next.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. Context engineering 101: figure out where the “dumb zone” begins. </span></strong><span>As a rule of thumb, the less of the context window that is used, the better the outcomes are. This is because the attention mechanism </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42717e90-129f-41cf-a96e-9cf8597629ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is quadratic</span></a><span>: the more that goes into the context window, the more compute is required to process it all. </span><em><span>We cover more about self-attention scalability challenges </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42717e90-129f-41cf-a96e-9cf8597629ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in our ChatGPT deepdive</span></a><span>.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For a model with a 1M context window, Dex pushes it to around 300-400K when it feels right. For smaller models, he stops at around 100K. You hit the “dumb zone” when its performance starts to degrade because the context window fills up beyond this heuristic limit, and the model begins doing increasingly stupid things like deleting your .env file, for example.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. A larger context window does not mean a smarter model. </span></strong><span>Models’ intelligence is behind the ability to use the tokens in the context window, by deciding which parts of the context are relevant for the next decision. You have to get a feel for how much context usage makes sense, and experiment when you hit the “dumb zone.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Frequent, intentional compaction is a technique Dex uses for more complex projects. </span></strong><span>He will take a long and noisy context, compress it into a Markdown document, then start a new session fresh, pointing the model to this “compressed context” that is in the Markdown.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A workflow he uses:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>One session reads a ton of code (filling up its context window while in the “smart zone”), then emits a research document</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The next session takes tickets describing the work to be done and turns it into a design document</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The following session takes both documents to create a plan</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The human is in the loop where it </span><em><span>really</span></em><span> matters: in this case, reviewing the design document and architecture because Dex finds models to be weak on this</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Don’t bother optimizing LLM usage until business is booming, there’s massive scale, or high costs. </span></strong><span>Dex suggests to always start building software with the smartest available model to solve the problem, since engineering time is almost always the bottleneck. Begin to optimize LLM usage and context usage only when at real scale and costs are high enough. That’s when it can be worth using GPT-OSS-120B (1/1,000th the cost of Opus) for the simpler steps in your process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. “You’re completely right!” or “you’re right to push back on that” are phrases that mean it’s time to start a new session. </span></strong><span>These responses mean the LLM session is trajectory-poisoned, and you’re wasting time and tokens to continue. Models are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a97b784-a793-4b3f-988a-5b9a82c75ff4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>autoregressive</span></a><span>, so if you get into this loop of:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model makes a mistake</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ user “yells”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ model keeps making mistakes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ user “yells”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… the model calculates that the next most probable message is to make another mistake!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Only four things matter in the context window:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Size</span></strong><span>: the bigger it is, the more space you should have before hitting the “dumb zone”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Information quality</span></strong><span>. Once something is in the context window, every subsequent turn treats it as fact. This is why errors can compound.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Missing information</span></strong><span>: if there’s information missing that the agent would need, the outcome will be worse, as the agent fills in the gap with guesses.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Trajectory. </span></strong><span>Models are autoregressive, so they predict the next message in the conversation based on previous ones in a kind of thread of reasoning. “Trajectory poisoning” is when the agent gets into a pattern of doing things you don’t want. In this case, it’s time to start over.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Slow loops are Dex’s favorite way to do ‘loop engineering.’ </span></strong><span>The HumanLayer team started with a nightly automation setup that kicks off an agent to fix one thing in the codebase, and open a pull request. In the mornings, they woke up to a PR waiting to be merged. They tweaked it over time and now have four agents open a total of four PRs by the morning, with the focus on code quality improvements. A person still reads all of them before merging.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. “Token harder” vs. “token smarter”:</span></strong><span> Dex is in a group chat named ‘Hyper Engineering’, where members share advice on how to max out their Claude subscriptions. This approach, he calls “token harder”. On the other side is “token smarter”: aiming to get maximum value from AI while keeping control. Smarter is harder to pull off.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>12. Three ways to run a “software factory.” </span></strong><span>Here’s options Dex sees as viable:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>“Turn the lights off:</span></strong><span>” go all-in on agentic coding, do not review the code, and pray that AI doesn’t create too much slop. </span><em><span>Dex tried this and failed.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Read and review all AI-generated code. </span></strong><span>This slows things down to human speed. Dex says that this way, you should expect a 30-50% lift in productivity from AI, compared to pre-AI engineering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Find leverage, but keep people in the loop. </span></strong><span>Find out where an hour spent in planning could save four hours’ worth of implementation, in terms of fewer bugs. Invest more time in areas with leverage: design, architecture, and key decisions. Then, let the agent generate code and don’t insist on reviewing all of it. In this way, Dex believes you can move 2-3x faster than when devs wrote all code by hand.</span></p></li></ol><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro This means an increase in automated answers with less human intervention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, the cases handled automatically are largely lookups and routine changes that map cleanly onto a structured workflow. The cases that remain are typically disputes, such as a host and a guest having different views about a cancellation. In such cases, the travel platform is positioned between them and is accountable for the funds. The platform needs to figure out how to deal with these cases. It is not just a business problem, but also an engineering problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is an important question at the center of this problem. At what moment should the system stop and route a case to a human agent?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A platform fielding hundreds of millions of contacts a year faces that decision millions of times a day, across cancellations, refunds, and after-hours lockouts. A confident but wrong answer can ruin a traveler’s trip and the money at stake.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Airbnb, Booking[dot]com, and Expedia have each tried to solve this problem in different ways. Airbnb prioritized autonomous resolution, building models that settle cancellations and refunds before an agent enters the conversation. Booking concentrated on the handoff, routing complex cases to a representative briefed in advance while equipping hosts to answer guests directly. Expedia emphasized deflection at scale, investing in summaries that carry context across more than thirty languages so an escalated case arrives intact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look more closely at the different solutions by following the support pipeline from first principles, show why a tail of cases resists automation regardless of model quality, and use these three approaches to understand how these can be handled.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Pipeline</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Start with the simplest version of automated support: a bot that matches a traveler’s message to a list of frequently asked questions and returns the closest article.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It works for questions like “What is your cancellation policy?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, it fails the moment a traveler writes something like “My host agreed to refund me, so what happens if I cancel now?” That sentence carries an intent, a history, and a financial consequence, and a simple keyword match treats it as a search query.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The first real component is intent detection. In plain terms, the system classifies the message and identifies what the traveler wants: a rebooking, a refund, or a question about an existing reservation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Airbnb frames this as a layered problem:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A top-level model performs domain classification, sorting the message into a broad category such as cancellation or a help-article question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Once the category is settled, a second layer of domain-specific models takes over to work out the details.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For a cancellation, those second-layer models answer focused questions. Did the host or the guest initiate it? Have both sides agreed on a refund amount?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Alongside this, a separate model predicts the expected refund ratio (such as the share of the payment a human agent would typically return given the circumstances of the trip). That predictor is trained on years of past agent decisions, which lets the system produce decisions in line with how experienced staff have handled similar cases.</span></p><div justify"><span>However, a message understood is still inert until two further capabilities exist:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The system tracks state, meaning it carries the context of earlier messages in the thread, so a follow-up reply makes sense against what came before.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>And it has an action layer, the part wired into live systems that can issue the refund, move the reservation, or open the mutual cancellation flow.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Reading intent is the easier half. Taking a correct, reversible action against live booking and payment systems is what requires greater consideration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The final element is a confidence threshold. Each prediction arrives with a score, and the threshold determines whether the system proceeds on its own or routes the case to a person. If this bar is set too low, more cases clear automatically while errors creep upward. If it is raised, the accuracy improves, but more traffic lands on human agents. That single threshold value is where much of the tuning happens</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This pipeline, intent detection, state tracking, an action layer, and a confidence threshold, handles a large volume of everyday requests well. However, it keeps facing problems in one family of cases.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Adjudication</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The cases that clear automatically share a quality. They are answerable by retrieval.  In other words, the system finds a fact or applies a rule, such as the status of a refund or the steps to change a date. Volume here is high, and the work is repetitive. These are the types of problems where automation works well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The cases that resist automation differ in kind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>They require adjudication, meaning a judgment between parties whose accounts and interests diverge. A guest says the apartment was misrepresented. The host says the listing was accurate and the guest simply changed their mind. A damage claim sits between them, and the platform holds the deposit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There are three parties, three versions, and one decision about money. A better model produces a cleaner summary of the dispute, yet the underlying call still rests on weighing competing claims, which is difficult for even a powerful model.</span></p><div justify"><span>Time pressure sharpens the divide.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When flights were cancelled across the Middle East, and a surge of travelers contacted Expedia at once, automation absorbed the routine rebookings and status checks at speed, which freed human agents to spend their attention on the tangled, time-sensitive cases. The same event produced both kinds of work in the same minutes, and the value of the split was that each kind reached the right handler.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is why the resolution rate climbs and then flattens. The boundary separating automated from escalated cases advances as retrieval improves, and it approaches a region of adjudication-heavy cases that stay with people by design.</span></p><div justify"><span>It also explains why headline percentages deserve careful consideration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Airbnb reports that more than 40% of guest issues are resolved without an agent. Expedia reports that more than 30% of its self-service interactions are powered by AI, where self-service already accounts for more than half of all contacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Those two figures rest on different bases, so a side-by-side ranking would mislead more than it informs. Each number describes its own pipeline rather than a shared scoreboard.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Handoff</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When a case crosses to a person, the details of what is shared become important.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A handoff that passes along only “escalated, please assist” forces the customer support agent to restart the conversation, and the traveler retells the whole story to a second responder. A traveler who repeats every detail to a human after a stalled bot session ends up more frustrated than one who reached a person at the start.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This asymmetry is the reason handoff deserves real engineering attention. A weak handoff can leave the combined system performing worse than plain human support would.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The solution to this lies in the payload: the bundle of context that accompanies an escalated case. A strong payload carries four elements.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A summary of the conversation so far.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The structured facts already gathered include the booking reference and the cancellation reason.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The live state of the reservation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A translation, where the agent and the traveler use different languages.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The agent opens the case already informed and continues from where the automation left off.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Expedia leans on this idea at scale. Its systems generate conversation summaries across more than thirty languages, so a case handled partly in Portuguese can reach an English-speaking support agent with the thread rendered in a language they read fluently. The same summaries shortened the time required to bring new agents up to speed by a substantial margin, because a well-formed summary teaches as it informs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Booking describes the same priority from the other side. Its tools route complex questions to a representative who receives the relevant booking and property details in advance, so the human starts the conversation already holding the facts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Booking also adds a second component that the others treat as secondary. Much of its support volume is communication between a guest and an accommodation partner, so it built tooling that drafts partner replies from property and reservation data and suggests them to the host. Here, the friction is the message between two people rather than a decision the platform owes, and equipping the partner to answer quickly relieves pressure before a formal support case ever opens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The pattern across all approaches is consistent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The success path contributes to the headline percentage, while the failure path, the moment a case escalates, is where the overall customer experience is decided. The core work for building such systems concentrates on handoff far more than on the straightforward case where everything resolves on the first attempt.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Divergence</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The design decisions made by the three companies indirectly express three beliefs about which part of travel support is hardest.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Airbnb’s position is that the adjudication itself can be modeled. By training on the expected refund ratio and on the questions agents ask during a cancellation, it pushes the automated portion as far toward real decisions as the data supports, and it reserves human attention for safety, discrimination, and high-value claims. The wager is that a large share of disputes follow learnable patterns, and that an autonomous system applying a consistent standard serves travelers better than a queue of agents who each interpret a policy slightly differently. The cost of this position is a heavy, continuous investment in models and labeled data, and a high bar for caution wherever money and safety meet.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Booking solves the problem differently. Its emphasis on briefing the human agent and on drafting replies for partners treats communication as the primary friction. The implied belief is that a great deal of support volume is people struggling to reach each other, a guest with a question and a host with the answer, and that closing that gap quickly matters more than resolving every case autonomously. This keeps more humans in the loop while raising the quality of each human touch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Expedia’s emphasis on deflection and multilingual summaries reflects a third belief that scale is the dominant variable. With well over two hundred million interactions a year, even modest gains in self-service rates and handling times compound into large absolute numbers, so the architecture optimizes for volume routed correctly and for context that survives a language boundary across a global workforce.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every placement of the boundary carries a price on each side, and the confidence threshold makes the trade concrete.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Raise the threshold, and the system escalates more often, which guards against autonomous errors while increasing the load on human agents and the cost that comes with it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Lower the threshold, and the system resolves more cases on its own, which trims cost while admitting more mistakes in situations that involve money.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is an operating point that balances the two, and choosing it requires judgment about how expensive an error is relative to an escalation. In travel, where an error can mean a wrongly denied refund on someone’s holiday, that judgment leans conservative wherever the stakes run high.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>There is also a more fundamental limit worth considering.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The chat interface itself suits travel poorly, because a chat thread is built for one person, while a travel dispute often involves several. A cancellation between a host and a guest, mediated by a platform, is a conversation among three parties, and a linear thread struggles to hold that arrangement sometimes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It is not simply a matter of improving the interface. It suggests that the format through which support arrives may bound how far automation can go, separate from how capable the model becomes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For that reason, regulated cases, high-value claims, and anything touching safety remain with people on purpose. The boundary moves rightward over time, and a margin is kept on the far side, where human judgment is meant to outweigh a confident automated answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The percentage of issues resolved without a human is an indication of two things: where a platform places its automate-versus-escalate boundary and how much of its work is answerable by retrieval rather than judgment. The model matters, yet it operates inside a structure built to manage that boundary.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A few points hold across all three platforms.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The pipeline serves the boundary. Intent detection, state tracking, the action layer, and the confidence threshold all feed the single decision to resolve a case or escalate it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The handoff decides the experience. A case that crosses to a person succeeds or fails on the context that travels with it, which is why summaries, structured facts, and reservations carry so much weight.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The placement encodes a belief. Airbnb bet on autonomous adjudication, Booking on communication and a briefed handoff, and Expedia on correctly routed scale, with each placement reflecting a different view of where travel support is hardest.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Put together, the resolution rate reflects a design decision as much as a level of capability, and the boundary is the part of the system worth reading first.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>“Loop engineering” has become a trending topic in the past month, after some high-profile folks At Anthropic’s developer conference, Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7f791600-49be-4e6b-9583-9fdd676a9605?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>said</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I don’t prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude and figuring out what to do. </span><strong><span>My job is to write loops.</span></strong><span>”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Soon after, Peter Steinberger, creator of OpenClaw, preached loop design in a post:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" underline;"><span>an article</span></a><span>, ‘Loop Engineering’:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Loop engineering is replacing yourself as the person who prompts the agent. You design the system that does it instead.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s three mentions in quick succession of this new approach, which is a novel one and therefore pretty abstract to me. To find out more, I turned online to some of the folks who read these articles. In replies, you told me what “loop engineering” means to you and gave some examples of loops in your work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Where it began: “Ralph Wiggum” loop.</span></strong><span> A year ago, software engineer Geoffrey Huntley shared how he builds “loops.” In December, the approach went viral and “Ralph loops” were born.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>The /goal command ships in all major harnesses.</span></strong><span> By May this year, the major AI coding harnesses added support to run a loop from a single prompt, using the /goal command.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Loops which devs use: triggers and cron jobs.</span></strong><span> I asked devs how they use loops. Most use cases involve responding to events or running scheduled jobs. They are useful, but don’t feel like brand new workflows.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Helpful loops for devs. </span></strong><span>Open PRs for newly-recorded app issues, have notes ready when an oncall joins an outage Slack channel, “babysitting” and fixing nightly end-to-end tests, and more.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Disappointment and “tokenmaxxing”</span></strong><span>. Several devs reject looping after trying it. Agents drifting, and the “human in the loop” having better results are some reasons. Also, at companies that pay API prices for tokens, loop engineering gets expensive fast.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Was looping a hack while tooling caught up?</span></strong><span> Distinguished engineer Max Kanat-Alexander believes the “loop” might have just been a temporary hack while the harnesses added the ability to do the same from a single prompt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Does “context engineering” matter more for devs? </span></strong><span>Except for engineers building AI infra, there seems little benefit in going deep into loop engineering. Instead, becoming familiar with AI context windows – also part of building loops – could be more useful.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Where it began: “Ralph Wiggum” loop</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Exactly a year ago, software engineer Geoffrey Huntley published the article ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/195bb6a5-2c53-4ec1-a109-969c285b4fcd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer</span></a><span>’. The name references the naive son of the local police chief in The Simpsons, who is extremely eager to always be helpful. In engineering, “Ralph” is intended to continuously nudge the agent in the right direction. Geoff described it:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Ralph is a technique. In its purest form, Ralph is a Bash loop:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ralph can replace the majority of outsourcing at most companies for greenfield projects. It has defects, but these are identifiable and resolvable through various styles of prompts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s the beauty of Ralph - the technique is deterministically bad in a nondeterministic world.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The article expands on the idea of the Ralph loop:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start the agent with a prompt that captures the task and defines a goal</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start loops if needed: spawn subagents as and when necessary</span></p></li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: There is no way this is possible without senior expertise guiding Ralph. A Goal gives Codex a completion condition: what should be true, how success should be checked, and what constraints must stay intact.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also from the docs (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“A normal prompt says: do this next thing.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A Goal says: keep working until this outcome is true.</span></strong><span> In a normal request, Codex works through the immediate instruction, reports a result, and waits. With a Goal, Codex has a durable target attached to the thread. After a turn finishes, it can inspect the current evidence and decide whether the objective is satisfied. If the answer is no, and the Goal remains active and within budget, Codex can continue from the latest state.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: So, how did OpenAI build Goals? They used files, logs, running tests, and lifecycle controls:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
