Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba9a03f8-d7df-4457-af94-ce62a3a9ac91?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>OpenAI</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In this way, “Goals” feels awfully similar to a Ralph loop, except compressed into a single command! </span></strong><span>It feels like the Codex team took the idea of the Ralph loop, built infrastructure around it, took care of coordinating agents by not having them step on one another, dealt with state, running of tests, starting and stopping agents, and then added functionality such as being able to set a budget.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>May: Hermes and Claude Code follow with /goal</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three days later (May 2), Hermes agent, a popular AI agent framework and OpenClaw rival, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/db12b265-032e-41f6-b77c-36c01ab936d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shipped</span></a><span> their implementation of /goal. From the docs:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“[/goal] It’s our take on the Ralph loop, directly inspired by Codex CLI 0.128.0’s /goal by Eric Traut (OpenAI). The core idea — keep a goal alive across turns and don’t stop until it’s achieved — is theirs. The implementation here is independent and adapted to Hermes’ architecture.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Less than two weeks later – on 12 May – Claude Code also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6cf127e2-8ba2-41d3-96dd-4372d6db0eae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shipped</span></a><span> their /goal command. It’s identical in what it does to Codex. From Claude Code:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The /goal command sets a completion condition and Claude keeps working toward it without you prompting each step. After each turn, a small fast model checks whether the condition holds. If not, Claude starts another turn instead of returning control to you. The goal clears automatically once the condition is met.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few months before, in March, Claude Code shipped the concept of scheduling an agent with the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/199d14ea-4441-476b-a0fb-4367db5373c6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>/loop command</span></a><span>. It is basically what JavaScript’s setTimeout() function would be equivalent to: repeat a task after a given interval until the work is done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>By May, running a Ralph loop had become as simple as giving a single command in one of the major agent harnesses. </span></strong><span>It’s as if AI labs noticed user demand to do more with agentic loops which were hard to set up, and built ways to make it simpler. For instance, in open source agent harnesses like OpenCode, there are plugins like the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1b105a63-6dbe-416d-95ca-1cee59d396ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>/goal plugin</span></a><span>. For the minimalist coding agent, Pi, the /goal command can be added </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed24d4e6-8823-48d1-a754-df46a978b08a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as a package.</span></a></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Loops which devs use: triggers and cron jobs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By May, we had access to the /goal primitive. So, what use cases were Boris Cherny and Peter Steinberger referring to in terms of spending most of their time on designing loops, instead of writing prompts? I asked around for examples of “loop engineering” from fellow devs. Based on ~210 replies, mostly from X and LinkedIn, it seems that triggers and cron jobs are two very common use cases for loop engineering:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Triggers / automations</span></strong><span>: an agent kicks off when an event happens. The event could be an error being logged, a new ticket created, customer support feedback received, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pre-AI, these events were typically triggered by a webhook, and kicked off things like a Slack bot posting in a channel, triggering a system, or being the starting point of a Zapier or an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c41cd4e9-591c-4083-b565-5cc9ff2eda69?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>n8n</span></a><span> integration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Cron jobs: </span></strong><span>many devs see “loop engineering” as kicking off jobs that involve agents on a cadence. This is fundamentally the same as scheduled </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/151b3b67-86a2-4f9f-8dfe-f8fe8ed72812?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>cron jobs</span></a><span>. From director of engineering, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/90023f42-b36c-44d2-af92-3d7d95a96090?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Oded Messer</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The idea is that strategic workflows that are repeatable and automatable can be done so with an agent. OK. But if my strategic workflow is automatable then it either becomes tactical if the AI is capable enough or it’s just a high level old-school-automation I can set up like a cron or a trigger.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The name suggests simplicity and repetition. Sometimes it feels like AI enthusiasts forgot automation was a thing before LLMs.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Helpful loops for devs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Below are some workflows with AI agents that run on a regular basis as a /loop command, or when triggered:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Development-related work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Open PRs for newly recorded app issues. </span></strong><span>Software engineer </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b88cb55d-6184-4fad-8ad8-da64b3b02be7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ivan Pantić</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>“App encounters a problem and creates a sentry issue. Then:</span><br><span>→ Cron tells agent to check sentry and open PRs.</span><br><span>→If there’s no active PR, agent tackles the issue and creates one</span><br><span>→ If PRs aren’t reviewed, agent pings the devs via slack</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this flow, there is only one PR open at a time.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Fix flakey tests. </span></strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71a7e2e7-6f51-4bec-a890-b1386b52ec42?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Paul D’Ambra</span></a><span>, software engineer at PostHog:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“/loop pull the next flakey test from the trunk API. run it to check if it flakes locally, if it does open a PR with the fix... which netted me 13 PRs to stabilise some of our tests.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Triaging issues and outages. </span></strong><span>Software engineer </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/52c7146f-3ccc-4bb3-b9a2-1842fbc4cc09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ivan Abad:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>“A new alert/exception pops up in a channel. </span><br><span>→ The agent investigates the issue</span><br><span>→ if it is a code change, implements the change</span><br><span>→ creates the PR </span><br><span>→ pings the human for review. </span><br><br><span>Same applies for customer tickets or incidents. By the time you get paged and connect to the incident the agent already triaged everything and often located the root cause.”</span></span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Review design plans. </span></strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6431ace6-1f8b-4f8e-8b8d-55974ea14a7e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Artem Nikitin</span></a><span>, software engineer at Elastic:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“What I’m finding myself doing often recently is to review design/implementation plans in a loop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Usually, agents only find a few issues during a normal run and then find more on subsequent runs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So I’m now asking them to run in a loop until they find 0 new major issues.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Daily/nightly work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Daily product improvements. </span></strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c4a6489a-0b07-440b-a9c1-a9ef717222b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jack D,</span></a><span> founding engineer at Schematic:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We have a loop which reads the logs for the last 24 hours, user feedback and makes PR with fixes - we still review the PRs it makes though!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Nightly end-to-end test run babysitted by an agent. </span></strong><span>Utku K, engineering manager:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“nightly e2e runs on the frontend app. When a test fails, an agent investigates first to work out whether it’s a real regression or a false negative. If it’s a real bug, the agent attempts a fix, reruns the test, and keeps iterating until it passes or hits a retry cap and escalates... Either way it lands as a PR ready for review by morning.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>More complex development work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Build new telemetry integrations and verify they work</span></strong><span>. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ee1b5dc-d090-4931-b702-9d6b35f75331?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Lawrence Jones</span></a><span>, software engineer at Incident.io:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A lot of the AI runbook that we use to build new telemetry integrations uses loops such as executing the query, verifying that it executed correctly and iterating on the query plan/output format/whatever until it is happy with the outcome.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Do a long-running migration, mostly autonomously</span></strong><span>. Startup founder </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fea339ac-7a47-439f-86ab-f80bc8e52038?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Rafel Mendiola</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Recently, I converted my startup’s codebase from a regular React app to a React Native app using Expo.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two ways I could have done it:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In the traditional software engineering style, I could have created a large epic with 50-100 different tickets. I started building myself the infrastructure for that, it felt like it was way too much work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What I did instead was create a skill that would let an agent figure out a small to medium-sized piece of work or piece of code to convert, given certain detection mechanisms and guidelines, and then do that conversion and keep track of the migration progress. Then I put that skill on a cron job. This was a lot easier to handle cognitively than managing a large migration plan. It also ran every 30 minutes, not nightly or weekly.”</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Productivity-related workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Daily tasks executed. </span></strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3143e70d-19e1-4cf6-9096-da54daa58717?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Aaron Stannard</span></a><span>, creator of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/613435ab-28eb-4a86-b9bc-50265dcfd437?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Akka.NET</span></a><span>:</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I use a reminder with my Netclaw instance to run both engineering and non-engineering things in a loop:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>1. Daily CRM triage </span><br><span>2. Support ticket SLA monitoring </span><br><span>3. Disk space management on my dev box </span><br><span>4. Triaging dependent PRs”</span></span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Daily and weekly automations. </span></strong><span>From founder and product manager </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/adfedb71-efc2-49a0-b430-17bab1e3f2aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Matt Teixeria</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I have 4 main loops:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Daily: Decision Log Loop. → It writes to a Slack channel about what decisions have been taken, still yet to be taken, and any possible blockers by looking at Granola, Jira, and a few other tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Weekly: Customer Feedback Review → Queries all insights created in the past week in Deck</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Weekly: Post Feature Implementation Check in →After releasing a feature, it looks at analytics, feedback, bugs etc</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Weekly: Product Market Fit Checker → goes over last week’s PMF survey and synthesizes actions to take “</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Disappointment and “tokenmaxxing”</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Plenty of devs shared that they tried loops but that it didn’t help them. Some common observations:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Human in the loop” works a lot better than letting the agent run by itself.</span></strong><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c9b1185-df4b-4426-9b7e-f94b3efdb024?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Kyle Straits</span></a><span>, founder at Stratis Data Labs:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I avoid loops. I had okay results with Ralph loops but nothing beats some well-defined skills, human in the loop (HITL), and an appropriate number of tools”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Lack of trust in the agent.</span></strong><span> Lead software engineer </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5c253f88-c90f-4d98-b080-515822aa476d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Anitha Mittapalli</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I find AI drifting or going off course several times and can’t trust it 100%. I use it every day, but still remain as an orchestrator.  It all depends on the type of tasks or problems you are solving. Thing is, work that is visual, subjective, architectural, or requires a lot of real-time design pivots, doesn’t always work well with autonomous agents or looping.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d9238f67-012c-42c9-96e3-090df974160d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jose Salvatierra</span></a><span>, founding engineer at Paper Run says the same:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Loops are handy for simple/low context tasks but it seems to break down as soon as things get complex and you need to guide the agent.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s hard to have a clear success criteria for complex work. </span></strong><span>Fractional CTO, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/24a29ac7-0ea9-4caa-bee5-4526e370281a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Carly Rector</span></a><span>, explains:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Complicated tasks rarely have clear success criteria you can fully define upfront... The examples of coding agents going away for weeks to build an [X] tend not to mention the time it takes to build the spec you give it... the job of specifying what you want to build is definitionally your job.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Why ‘loop engineer’ when tokens cost money?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A point of view exists that “loop engineering” is about incentivizing </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1402f920-39e7-4643-b083-6693a974c2c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>tokenmaxxing</span></a><span>. Plenty of devs spoke of their suspicion that AI labs are driven to incentivize more token usage, while loop engineering requires spending a lot of tokens. Plus, this new way of working is promoted from inside of OpenAI and Anthropic. Hence, there’s this suspicion that loop engineering is a plot to enrich AI labs by driving token usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true the incentives align, but I wonder if it’s something else:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Could it be that “designing loops” is more popular within AI labs because token budgets are absent there? </span></strong><span>Inside these places, devs are incentivized to experiment however they want.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, token costs are a concern elsewhere, and more places are</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c7f2871-2261-41cf-bfce-b184efcaa9bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> cutting back on token spend.</span></a><span> Devs on subsidized Claude Code and Codex plans will use primitives like /goal to start longer-running tasks, while those on a budget will consider the cost of the loop more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also where the idea of running open models on your own infra becomes more interesting because in this setting, the model is effectively “free” beyond the fixed setup fee, and suddenly tokenmaxxing (using GPUs at full capacity) is no longer economically silly!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Was looping a hack while tooling caught up?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Talking with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf842d32-1633-4712-bd38-c9f5a85addff?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Max Kanat-Alexander</span></a><span> – an executive distinguished engineer at Capital One, and formerly of LinkedIn – he made an interesting observation about how model shops keep improving their tooling:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think about the incentives that the model shops have in the long run. Those incentives always seem to be squarely aligned with “support people writing a single vague prompt and giving them what they want, without them having to do anything special or understand anything about the tool.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to me that anything you have to know about the tool would eventually become baked into its default workflow (or model capability would overtake it) if it really does get genuinely validated.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I agree with Max, OpenAI and Anthropic seem very good at launching DIY tools that take off because something is missing in Codex or Claude Code that needs a workaround. They simply build a version of the workaround into their products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps this points to why the loop engineering trend looks like being short-lived: if you have an ambitious project with a measurable goal, you can now one-shot it in a harness, and have long-running agents swarm and attempt to build it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Max had another sage point about why trends like “Ralph loops” and “loop engineering” might not last long:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s a theme of the last few years: there’s a trend that people get excited about which is then obviated because if it’s completely right, the model shops will inherently integrate it.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Does “context engineering” matter more for devs?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the time of publication, “loop engineering” seems as good as obsolete for most of us software engineers who build “regular” software. The tools have caught up and we can use the /goal or /loop prompts to do more ambitious, verifiable, tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But I reckon that designing loops will remain an important task at the AI infra level – and is probably why engineers at AI labs talk about it so much. </span></strong><span>It would be quite a lot of work to build a Ralph loop from scratch that you can ship in an AI harness like Codex, or a solution that’s resilient to a node running a crashing agent, is secure enough, auditable, etc. But if you do build this, you’ll learn plenty:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to decide when to start subagents, and how many of them to kick off</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to store the “global state” of the run: in files, memory, or in some other storage?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to avoid agents stepping on each other when working; for example, by using worktrees, working in the same filesystem but on different files, or something else?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How much of the context window to use, when to do </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d81f086-3f9d-4d48-b394-576a8481a375?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>context compaction/compression</span></a><span>, and other related stuff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and you’d solve many interesting problems!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Understanding “context engineering” can be useful when working with LLMs. </span></strong><span>Interest in Ralph loops started because the context window of LLMs is too small to hold large codebases, and with long-running, complex work the context window fills up. Also, the more you fill the context window, the less useful the LLM becomes because more errors compound and the agent “drifts.” Here’s my attempt at visualizing this:</span></p><div 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Loop engineering: a rebrand of triggers and scheduled jobs used for decades?</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that would be a little unfair.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The reason “loop engineering” no longer matters for most devs is because AI harnesses are very quick in “one-shotting” more complex workflows. </span></strong><span>A year ago, it took a 30-minute read from Geoffrey Huntley to understand the theory of Ralph loops, and devs spent hours putting together their own looping environments. Then, Codex, Claude Code, and other AI harnesses built this functionality and abstracted it behind a simple command.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>So now, all complexity has been removed, and most devs no longer need to know much about looping or playing with context windows, unless building a harness, or needing to build a similar infra piece from scratch.</span><br><br></span><strong><span>A note of caution: there is a large amount of misleading AI slop on social media about loop engineering, so it helps to be able to spot the nonsense. </span></strong><span>Indeed, working on this article was the first time I have nearly fallen for AI replies to a mini-survey I ran on social media. I got lots of replies hyping up loop engineering, but offering no specifics. Sure enough, when I looked closer at the accounts posting these replies, they looked like they’re run by an AI bot. Here’s a couple such replies about loop engineering:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The loop is what runs when you’re not typing. it’s the agent deciding what to try next, running it, reading the result, deciding again. you’re not writing the steps anymore, you’re writing the objective and the constraints. that’s the paradigm shift” – AI-nonsense reply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/23052c49-514d-463e-a86f-225529395ba8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>from a founder</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Workflows have existed for years. What’s new is who owns the next step. In a traditional workflow, every stage waits for a person to decide what happens next. In a loop, the agent keeps planning, verifying, and correcting itself until it hits a stopping condition or asks for human judgment.” – another founder </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7168b3d-c462-419b-9dc6-311041c4b258?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>posting AI nonsense</span></a><span>.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s not just AI nonsense, but those posting about “loop engineering” are hard to relate as a “normal” software engineer. Here’s an “everyday” software engineer who experiments with AI, a lot, telling me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I feel a strange disconnect with the folks running loops. I usually cannot get my LLM to write even 200 - 500 lines without doing some major idiocy like returning a “fallback value” instead of an error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But on Twitter/X it’s a parallel reality where nobody writes or reads any code and runs 100 loops. I keep asking myself: am I doing it wrong?”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To this engineer: you’re probably not doing it wrong, but loops are not “magic” for most of us. </span><em><span>If you’re working building AI infra-like projects where you’re creating new, loop-like building blocks with agents doing clever stuff that was not possible before, this probably doesn’t apply to you.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope this walkthrough of loop engineering and its demise at the hands of progress – and the fact it appears to be disappearing as fast as it appeared – was useful. Do leave a comment on how you use “loops” and any use cases I missed.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwNzA0Mzc3NiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODQwNDkwNzEsImV4cCI6MjA5OTYyNTA3MSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.CP64l6k9PqatWnaAMblFmK_m_9-kjeJ7YeOtTlilINg?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. It might offer a terse one-liner or a careful walk-through. It might sound fully confident, or it might hedge. Somewhere in training, the model learned which version you would rather have, even though both answers are correct.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That points to a harder question. How do you teach a model to be helpful when helpfulness changes with every request?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For a quick factual query, helpful means brevity. For a debugging problem, it means thoroughness. For a medical worry, it means caution paired with clarity. Each case requires a different direction with underlying trade-offs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The model learned to handle those trade-offs from people comparing answers thousands of times over. This idea of learning from comparison rather than from a fixed answer key sits beneath every popular model you have used.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at how that learning actually happens, starting with why instruction-following alone falls short, then walking through the two main methods for teaching preferences (RLHF and DPO).</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro justify"><span>Let’s look at each stage in a bit more detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first stage is pretraining. The model reads an enormous amount of text and learns to predict the next word. In other words, it builds a broad sense of how language works and soaks up world knowledge along the way. What it gains is raw capability. What it still lacks is direction, because predicting the next word and answering your question are two different goals.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second stage is supervised fine-tuning, or SFT. We show the model thousands of example pairs, each an instruction together with a good response, and train it to imitate them. After this stage, the model follows instructions instead of continuing text. For example, if we ask a model to summarize a paragraph, it writes a proper summary. A raw model without SFT would have rambled on.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third stage teaches preferences, which will be the focus of the rest of this article.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Why does a model that already follows instructions need a third stage at all?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is because SFT works through imitation. The model sees a correct answer and learns to copy its shape, which holds up well when a question has one good answer, but runs into problems when a question has many possible answers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Consider a request like “explain how a hash map works”. A short answer and a long answer can both be excellent, and which one helps depends on who is asking. An example dataset can show one of those answers, while the trade-off between them stays invisible. Imitation teaches the model what a good answer looks like, but struggles to teach it how to weigh two good answers against each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The payoff is larger than it might appear at first. For example, when OpenAI built InstructGPT in 2022, human raters preferred answers from a 1.3 billion parameter aligned model over answers from the 175 billion parameter GPT-3, a model roughly a hundred times larger. The alignment stage mattered more than a hundredfold jump in size.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Nevertheless, the line between pretraining and SFT is cleaner in the example than in practice.  Some recipes blend the two, but the three-stage view is the right place to start.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Next up, we need a signal that captures the trade-off directly. That signal is comparison.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0fd3b3d6-fce9-471a-915d-fe0f15b0dcec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Introducing Attio: the agentic CRM. style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reason this works comes down to what people are good at. Writing the single ideal response to a tricky prompt is hard, and two skilled people would produce different versions. Judging which of two responses is better is far easier, and people agree with each other more often when they compare than when they create. This is why labeling teams compare outputs instead of writing perfect ones from scratch, which makes the data trustworthy enough to train on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the same comparison data InstructGPT collected, and the starting point for both methods we are about to compare. They differ in what they do with it, while the comparisons stay the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To clarify, the comparisons can come from another AI model in place of a person, an approach used in RLAIF and Constitutional AI. The overall mechanics stay the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us now look at the two different methods.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>RLHF</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>RLHF, short for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, learns from comparisons by training a separate scorer and then coaching the model to score well against it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the below diagram that shows the basic RLHF flow:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/47d74cf8-aa89-47d0-b430-3f9ffeb5f85c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It works in two moves once the comparisons are collected.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>First, we train a reward model. We take those prompt-with-a-winner examples and train a separate model to score any response, high for the kind people preferred and lower for the kind they passed over. The reward model turns scattered human judgments into a single function that grades fresh responses on its own.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Second, we use that scorer to improve the main model, which here we call the policy. The policy writes a response, the reward model scores it, and a reinforcement learning algorithm called PPO nudges the policy toward higher-scoring responses.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Reinforcement learning, in plain terms, means learning from a reward signal through trial and error in place of labeled examples. Run the loop many times, and the policy drifts toward the answers people prefer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Left to chase a score freely, a model will discover strange, degenerate text that games the scorer while reading badly. To guard against that, we keep a frozen copy of the starting model, the reference, and penalize the policy whenever it strays too far from it. This penalty, the KL term, lets the policy improve while staying close enough to fluent language to stay useful.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reward model, the policy, the frozen reference, and a value model that PPO uses internally add up to four models in play during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That is the source of RLHF’s reputation for being expensive, fiddly, and slow to get right. However, this is also the pipeline behind the first version of ChatGPT, and it produced the first generation of genuinely helpful assistants at considerable cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Running a separate reward model and a full RL loop is a lot of moving parts. In 2023, a study from Stanford showed that much of it can collapse into a single step.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>DPO</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO reaches the same goal with the same data, replacing the reward model and the RL loop with one training step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO stands for Direct Preference Optimization, and the name fits. Rather than train a scorer and then optimize against it, the method tunes the model directly on the comparison pairs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The mechanics sit close to ordinary supervised learning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For each comparison, DPO adjusts the model to raise the probability of the preferred response and lower the probability of the rejected one, measured against that same frozen reference from before. The whole thing becomes a single loss that would train the way you would train a classifier. This is far simpler and steadier than an RL loop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A common idea is that DPO removes the reward model, but what actually happens is subtler. The Stanford paper that introduced DPO carries the idea in its title that a language model is secretly a reward model. The reward signal is still present, but it now lives inside the policy itself rather than in a separate network.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>The approach proved itself quickly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Zephyr, a 7 billion parameter model trained with DPO on machine-generated comparisons, beat Llama 2 Chat 70B, the strongest open RLHF model at the time, on a standard chat benchmark. Since then, DPO has become a staple in the industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>By folding the reward into a single training step, DPO put alignment within reach of a small team on a modest budget, far from any large research cluster. A family of variants, such as SimPO, KTO, and ORPO, adjusts the objective in different ways. They share DPO’s core approach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>On cost and simplicity, DPO looks like a clear win. The catch is one it shares with RLHF, and it sits in the signal both methods trust.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Reward Hacking</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both methods rely on a signal that only approximates human judgment, and leaning too hard on it can also backfire at times.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reward model, whether trained explicitly in RLHF or folded into the policy in DPO, is a proxy. It approximates what people prefer. Like any approximation, it also has gaps. Optimize the model hard against that proxy, and it can start to exploit those gaps. In other words, the score climbs while the answers get worse.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Researchers at OpenAI measured this directly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>As the model optimizes against the proxy, true quality rises for a while, then peaks and slides backward even as the proxy score keeps climbing. They tied it to Goodhart’s law, the old observation that a measure stops being a good measure once it becomes the target.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/24a34fbf-1837-46ef-99fe-62a4127694dd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" justify"><span>The everyday symptoms of this are familiar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Models pad answers with length because longer responses tend to score well, and they learn to agree with whatever view you express. This behavior is called sycophancy. Anthropic found that most of the time, both human raters and reward models prefer a confident, agreeable answer over a correct one, which sometimes means flattery in place of truth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The important part is that this trouble follows the data rather than the algorithm.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DPO inherits it just as RLHF does, because both learn from the same imperfect human judgments. Simpler training buys you a great deal, and this particular problem comes along for the ride. This is why your model sometimes agrees with you when you are clearly wrong. It learned that agreement tends to score well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The KL penalty we discussed earlier softens this by holding the model near its starting point, though it shrinks the problem rather than completely erasing it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the root trouble is an imperfect human signal, a natural question follows. Could we replace it with a signal that is exact? For a certain class of tasks, we can.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Verifiable Rewards</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When a program can check the answer, the human reward becomes optional, and that single fact reshaped the final training stages across 2025 and 2026.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some tasks have a checkable answer:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A math problem is right or wrong.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A piece of code passes its tests or fails them.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For these, we can replace the human-derived reward model with a verifier, a program that grades the result directly. The signal becomes exact and effectively free, clearing the proxy problem at its root for that work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>DeepSeek pushed this idea furthest.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>They introduced an RL method called GRPO that drops one of the extra models PPO needs, and they trained their R1 reasoning model largely by rewarding correct final answers on math and code. The results matched the strongest closed reasoning models of the time. The model learned to reason by checking its own work, guided by a reward a calculator could supply.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The limit is that a verifier can grade a math proof. However, it stays silent on whether an answer is honest, kind, or appropriately cautious. Those qualities take many acceptable forms and resist any automatic test, the territory preference learning was built for. DeepSeek themselves kept reward models for the helpfulness and safety parts of R1, while verifiable rewards drove the reasoning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This gives us the rule for the whole landscape.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>When a machine can check the answer, reach for verifiable rewards. When the answer is a matter of judgment, reach for preference learning, whether RLHF or DPO. The method follows the signal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is why reasoning models improved so quickly, and why even the best of them still rely on preference methods to stay pleasant and safe. Newer methods, such as DAPO and RLVR, extend the verifiable-reward idea, and they make up much of the active frontier in 2026.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We can retrace the path in a sentence each:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A raw model learns language and knowledge from pretraining.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Supervised fine-tuning teaches it to follow instructions by imitation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A third stage teaches preferences, because the questions that matter most often have several good answers and a real trade-off between them.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Comparison is the signal that captures that trade-off, and the two main methods both run on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>RLHF trains a separate reward model and optimizes against it with reinforcement learning, which is powerful and costly. On the other hand, DPO folds the same signal into a single training step, which is simpler and steadier while keeping the reward implicit rather than absent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Both inherit the same catch, that a human signal is a proxy, and pushing on it too hard breeds sycophancy and quiet failures. And when a task has a checkable answer, verifiable rewards now sidestep the proxy entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: item.title: Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams

Will Larson

“When you talk about growing an organization, the conversation usually leads to hiring. While I believe hiring is a very important approach to growing organizations, I believe we reach for it too often. In order to prioritize hiring for scenarios where it’ll do the most good, over the past year I’ve developed a loose framework for reasoning about what a given team needs to increase performance.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Staying On The Path To High Performing Teams

item.title: Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering

Brian Houck

“Each paper tackles a different question. Some measure the productivity impact of AI coding assistants. Others examine how those gains propagate through the software delivery process, explore what developers actually want from future AI systems, or reconsider the kinds of debt we should be paying attention to in an AI-assisted world. Despite coming from different research groups and using very different methodologies, they all seem to be converging on the same underlying story.”

#Management AI
item.description: Five Studies Changing How I Think About AI In Software Engineering

item.title: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

Steve Huynh

“After participating in many such conversations, both through my podcast and during my time at Amazon, I have recognized a handful of patterns that have held over the decades and across different companies. What follows is my running list of those patterns, the ones that keep surfacing whenever I sit down with someone elite. There are five of them, and I explain the gap between what they do and where most other people stop.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

item.title: Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t

“In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned.”

#IndustryTrends AI
item.description: Why AI Hasn’t Replaced Software Engineers, And Won’t

item.title: When AI Costs More Than The Engineer
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
When AI Costs More Than The Engineer

Tomasz Tunguz

“Anthropic spends 2.3x its payroll on compute — $515k per engineer per year at today's $224k fully-loaded salary. The top 1% of software companies spend $89k, the median $137. Three 2029 scenarios bracket how that gap closes.”

#Management
item.description: When AI Costs More Than The Engineer

item.title: On Data Quality
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
On Data Quality

Abraham Thomas

“Data quality. We love it, we want it, we praise it, we aspire to it. Even in these benighted and degenerate times, if there’s one belief that unites all sensible individuals, it is the belief that data quality is a Good Thing. It’s a pity, then, that nobody seems to know what data quality is.”

#DataEngineering Architecture
item.description: On Data Quality

Dr Andrew Leigh

A model update changes the agent’s behavior subtly, and nobody notices until a customer complains. Without identity controls, the agent runs as a shared system principal and there’s no audit trail when something goes wrong. Without guardrails, it confidently says something it shouldn’t. With Postgres, you change versions and you pretty much expect it to straight up work. Models are not like that. Each one has different properties that the harness has to adjust to. Agent Runtime</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Above the model is the agent runtime, which is what turns a model into an agent. The runtime handles the orchestration loop, the tool calls, the conversation state, and the protocol the rest of the harness speaks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not every step in that loop should run through the model. A well-built agent sends only the parts that need reasoning to the LLM and leaves the rest to ordinary code, since a database lookup or a purpose-built extraction model is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than asking a model to do the same work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The number of agent frameworks keeps growing, from open-source options like LangChain, LangGraph, and CrewAI to vendor-built runtimes. The principle that matters is framework neutrality. An agent built on one framework should be portable to another without rewriting the surrounding harness. Foundry, for example, lets agents run on any framework interchangeably.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure They need their own role assignments and their own audit trails, because a misbehaving agent has to be bounded by the same access controls that bound a misbehaving employee. The industry is still converging on how to do this well, and the answer most platforms are landing on is to extend an existing enterprise identity system to treat agents as a new class of principal rather than inventing a parallel system. For example, Foundry extends Entra, Microsoft’s enterprise identity platform, to treat agents this way. This is the access-control primitive; later in the article, the section on giving agents a place to act shows what an agent does once it has one of these identities.</span></p><div That’s the job of the context layer. While every other layer in the harness exists to let the agent run, context is what lets it run correctly. An agent without good context might hallucinate. It will give an answer, but the answer will be wrong in ways that are hard to detect because the agent itself doesn’t know what it doesn’t know. Marco was explicit that giving agents the context they need to actually work is one of the hardest problems his team is solving, and the one Microsoft is reasonably passionate about getting Classic RAG is a one-shot pattern. You take the user’s question, embed it, search a single index, return the top-k results, and pass them to the model. It works for simple questions against a small, clean corpus. It breaks the moment the question is ambiguous, the corpus is heterogeneous, the right answer requires combining sources, or the first retrieval comes back empty. The agent has no way to recover from a bad retrieval, and as Marco put it, when RAG isn’t working well, the whole agent isn’t working well. One-shot is the wrong shape for the problem.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 Two engineering ideas run through them. The first, retrieval-as-a-subagent, is the pattern behind all four. The second, giving an agent an identity and a place to act, is specifically what Work IQ adds on top of retrieval so that an agent can do work, not just find information.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Retrieval-as-a-Subagent</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The technical idea behind a production context layer is to wrap retrieval in an agentic loop. Instead of a single function call that runs one query against one index and returns the top-k, retrieval becomes a small agent of its own. It plans which sources to query, executes the queries, evaluates the results against the original question, and decides whether to return them, refine the query, or try a different source. Retrieval stops being a lookup and becomes an iterative process that can recover from a bad first pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Foundry IQ is the cleanest example of this in production today. The figure below shows the workflow when an agent calls it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
