justify"><span>Two naive options were present:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A database lookup on the hot path adds latency and a hard dependency on another service staying healthy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Routing to a random transceiver and forwarding internally works, but doubles the hop count.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI chose a third option.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The answer lives inside a field that WebRTC already exchanges. Every WebRTC session carries an ICE username fragment, called the ufrag, which is produced during session setup and echoed in STUN binding requests. STUN binding requests are the packets ICE uses to verify that two endpoints can actually reach each other, and they are usually the first thing a client sends on the media path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The trick is that OpenAI generates the server-side ufrag during signaling. They can put whatever they want in it, so they encode routing metadata into it. The relay parses just enough of the first STUN binding request to read the ufrag, decode the routing hint, and forward the packet to the transceiver that owns the session. Every packet after the first one flows through the established session mapping, which skips the ufrag parsing step entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below that shows the connection establishment sequence in detail:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>Each transceiver in the fleet listens on a shared UDP socket, which is one operating system endpoint bound to an internal IP and port. All sessions for that transceiver multiplex behind it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>During signaling, the transceiver returns a shared relay VIP and UDP port in the SDP answer. A VIP is a virtual IP address that fronts the entire relay fleet, so the client sees one stable destination like 203.0.113.10:3478, even though many relay instances sit behind that address. From the client’s side, there is one place to send packets, and it stays the same for the life of the session.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The relay’s state is purposefully tiny. It holds an in-memory map of source address to transceiver destination, plus some counters for monitoring and timers for session cleanup. If a relay instance restarts and loses the mapping, the next STUN packet rebuilds it from the ufrag. To make recovery faster, a Redis cache holds the source-to-destination mapping once a route is established. A restarted relay can look up the mapping from Redis immediately.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The principle here generalizes well. When we need data on the hot path, look at what the protocol is already exchanging. A field on the payload is essentially free to parse. A new lookup costs latency, a dependency, and one more thing that can break.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Global Relay and Geo-Steered Signaling</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once the public UDP surface was reduced to a small fixed set of addresses, the same relay pattern became deployable globally.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Global Relay is OpenAI’s fleet of geographically distributed relay ingress points. All of them run the identical packet-forwarding behavior described above. The only thing that changes is where on the map they sit.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Geographic distribution shortens the first client-to-OpenAI hop. A packet entering the network at a relay close to the user, in both geography and network topology, has a much easier time than a packet that has to traverse the public internet to reach a distant region first. The practical effect is lower latency, more stable timing, and a cleaner loss profile before traffic reaches the OpenAI backbone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI uses Cloudflare for geographic and proximity steering on the signaling side. The initial HTTP or WebSocket request that sets up a session is routed to a nearby transceiver cluster. The request context then determines which Global Relay ingress point gets advertised back to the client in the SDP answer. The ufrag carries enough information for Global Relay to route media to the right cluster, and for the cluster’s relay to route to the right transceiver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The result is that both the signaling and the media paths enter the OpenAI network at points close to the user, while the session itself stays anchored to one specific transceiver for its full lifetime. The setup round-trip and the first ICE connectivity check both shorten, which directly reduces how long a user waits before they can start speaking.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Go Relay Implementation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The relay is a Go service running in userspace, which is to say a regular process that reads from a regular UDP socket.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The Linux kernel receives UDP packets from the network interface, delivers them to a socket bound to the relay’s IP and port, and the Go process reads from that socket, updates a small amount of flow state, and forwards each packet to the right transceiver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI evaluated kernel-bypass frameworks (which let a userspace process poll the network card’s queues directly) and chose to stay away. Bypass raises packet throughput at the cost of operational complexity. The team’s workload fit inside what a careful Go implementation could handle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Three implementation choices carry most of the performance load.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">SO_REUSEPORT</span><span> is a Linux socket option that lets multiple workers on the same machine bind the same UDP port. The kernel then distributes incoming packets across those workers, which removes the bottleneck of a single read loop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">runtime.LockOSThread</span><span> pins each UDP-reading goroutine (a lightweight thread in Go) to a specific OS thread. Combined with </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">SO_REUSEPORT</span><span>, this tends to keep packets from the same flow on the same CPU core, which helps cache locality and reduces context switching.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Pre-allocated buffers and minimal copying during packet parsing keep allocation overhead low and avoid putting pressure on Go’s garbage collector.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The takeaway is that ordinary optimizations were enough. The relay handles OpenAI’s global real-time media traffic on a relatively small footprint.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Design Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every architecture comes with tradeoffs, and this one carries several worth understanding.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The whole design is built around 1:1 sessions. If OpenAI ever wants to add multiparty features (group voice calls, multiple participants in a single AI session, human handoff during a call), large parts of this architecture would probably need rework. Both the transceiver model and the choice to skip SFU rely on the assumption that most sessions have exactly two endpoints.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>OpenAI also took on a custom infrastructure burden. A standard SFU comes with documentation, a community, and battle-tested patterns. The relay, the transceiver, and the coordination between them are all internal code. Every engineer who works on this stack has to learn it from the inside out.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The “stateless” relay turns out to be stateless mostly in spirit. It holds an in-memory flow table and uses a Redis cache to recover that table across restarts. The architecture works because the protocol can rebuild the table from the ufrag, but the soft state is still a state.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Lastly, the ufrag trick depends on controlling both ends of signaling. OpenAI generates the server-side ufrag, so they can embed routing metadata in it freely. A team that uses an off-the-shelf signaling stack might find this technique harder to adapt directly.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The architecture OpenAI built for voice AI is a careful response to a specific pressure. WebRTC was designed for stable servers. Modern cloud infrastructure runs on the opposite assumption. OpenAI’s team had the protocol depth to determine whether a WebRTC session needs to live in one process at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Their answer separates the work into two pieces. A stateless relay forwards packets near the user. A stateful transceiver, anchored in one place, owns ICE, DTLS, SRTP, and the session lifecycle. The two pieces communicate through information that’s already in the WebRTC handshake, which keeps the routing decision on the packet path itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The implementation choices stayed deliberately simple. Userspace Go, </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">SO_REUSEPORT</span><span>, thread pinning, and careful memory management did the work that kernel bypass solves. The result handles 900 million weekly users on a relatively small relay footprint.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/440fee06-ab75-4c5e-b3a8-5eb924312be6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span>How Of course, at larger companies this setup is at least partially automated, but devs often need to do tweaking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No “tool context-switching.</span></strong><span>” Just mention it in Slack! Of course, opening Claude Code is not a big effort, but it’s still more work than just typing it out in Slack, and kicking off work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Routine work made easier.</span></strong><span> David has “Claude playing Pokémon” as his side project. Every time a new model comes out, he kicks off a run of his script on it. Previously, this took a few minutes to set up every time, and then it ran on his machine for hours. With this new Slack integration, it’s just one command.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My sense is that the excitement here is less about the Slack integration itself, and more to do with the fact that it’s easy to kick off one or more AIs that no longer run on a local machine. You can skip the setup entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>‘Claude Managed Agents’ is a big focus at Anthropic.</span></strong><span> While there, I met Katelyn Lesse, head of engineering for Claude Platform, who explained that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/46b35503-d03f-41f3-a681-cc2ce72a2da4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Claude Managed Agents</span></a><span> is a large, complex project which her team built over a six-month period. I also learned that cloud agents are becoming a big deal at OpenAI and Cursor, too.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>OpenAI bets big on Cloud Agents</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI acquired Ona, (formerly Gitpod), the leader in cloud development environments (CDEs). Back in 2021, CDEs were built for developers to develop software faster, and they also happen to be the perfect primitive for agents to run in a sandboxed cloud environment. From the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbcf1ff9-6b04-4136-8281-a63bb045b366?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>acquisition announcement by OpenAI</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As Codex becomes more capable, its most valuable work is unfolding over hours or days, rather than minutes. </span><strong><span>We believe people should be able to delegate more ambitious work without remaining tied to the machine where it began. </span></strong><span>The work should continue beyond the initial session, with Codex making it possible to stay connected and check progress, provide direction, make decisions, and review results from anywhere.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ona will help us do that. Its technology provides secure, persistent environments where agents can access the tools, systems, and context they need to make progress over time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By bringing Ona to OpenAI, we will expand Codex beyond work tied to a single device or active session and help more organizations deploy agents securely in production.“</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At OpenAI’s offices, I asked engineers there if their focus is shifting to cloud-based agents. Their answer: it very much is. This is a fairly recent development and they’re hiring engineers for the Cloud Agents team. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6586ac92-c2bd-4b10-ad2c-bd1f07425285?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>one job ad</span></a><span> that’s currently live:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We are looking for an experienced software engineer to help build and scale our cloud agent platform. You will design and operate systems for orchestrating agents at scale. You will work closely with product engineers on ChatGPT, API, and Codex to define the right abstractions and enable them to ship products quickly. Strong backend or infrastructure experience is important; experience with Python, Rust, distributed systems, cloud infrastructure, or product platforms is especially helpful.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Cursor: running agents in the cloud is the future</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Cursor, I spent an hour with cofounder Sualeh Asif (formerly the CTO, now Chief Product Officer). Cursor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce4af976-e7a7-4cb5-9649-7fad0f7c5c50?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>released Cloud Agents</span></a><span> at the end of last year, and is starting to focus a lot more on this area. Sualeh revealed some interesting details about working with cloud agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agents in the cloud don’t have a way to “complain.” </span></strong><span>With running an agent locally, when it gets warnings or errors, it surfaces them to a human in its response, who instructs it to do X or Y. However, there’s no such loop for a long-running task on the cloud! Cursor came up with the idea for the model “confess” in regular interviews, and the “confessions” are shared with the infra team to improve the agents’ environment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Long-running agents have their own challenges. </span></strong><span>What happens when a node terminates, midway through; how do you move agent execution from one node to the other? There are new, nontrivial engineering challenges the team needs to solve.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only yesterday, (Monday, 29 June), Cursor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2c42135c-0f39-4db4-b27e-4dce82320d7e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>launched</span></a><span> its iOS app that enables the building of software from anywhere.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/991a82d1-993c-4825-a4e1-df97eb713e8d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Cursor</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This product is built on top of cloud agents to allow for long-running tasks, the company said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Cloud agents run in isolated virtual machines with full development environments to test, verify, and demo work. Since they operate asynchronously with their own tools and resources, cloud agents can run for longer and iterate toward merge-ready PRs without intervention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To take advantage of these capabilities, send a local plan to a cloud agent or move active agents to the cloud to keep running. You can move the cloud session back to your computer to test changes locally before merging”.</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Why are cloud agents suddenly a thing?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It figures that running AI agents in the cloud is practical: there’s less setup involved, several can run in parallel, and the cloud is a better, more convenient place for long-running agents than a personal laptop is; i.e., having to keep the lid open even when walking around the office.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But why is this happening now? My hypothesis is that a mix of factors are at play:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Coding models got ‘good enough’. </span></strong><span>Before Opus 4.5 / GPT-5.4, AI models could not really code autonomously, so running them for long tasks was pointless!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Infra for AI coding agents has matured. </span></strong><span>Ways of giving more context to agents have improved: things like MCP and skills became mainstream and better understood.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>The context window is bigger.</span></strong><span> Today’s models have context windows of up to 1 million tokens, meaning that more complex instructions, code, and context can be passed in. It’s hard to have agents run for a longer time without access to a large context window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cloud providers have much more GPU capacity. </span></strong><span>Every cloud provider has been building GPU clusters in the last few years, and now there’s enough that these AI agents can make use of this infra.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Mass adoption of coding harnesses by non-developers?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At OpenAI, I also met </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45f864f6-7b5d-43e2-9ce7-64dae9f0b922?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Andrew Ambrosino</span></a><span>, who was the first engineer on the Codex team. Codex</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Almost everyone at OpenAI has switched from ChatGPT to Codex to get their work done! When I asked Kathleen Chaykowski, who works in Comms at the company, she said she uses Codex far more than ChatGPT, including for drafting presentations, conducting research, and brainstorming strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A separate notable detail in Andrew’s graph is that Engineering went from around 25% last September – when models had not yet significantly improved and Codex wasn’t as advanced – to 99% today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So, will non-engineering disciplines see equally rapid adoption of Codex-like tools, elsewhere? </span></strong><span>My sense is that the Codex team thinks the same will happen in other tech workplaces, so they’re preparing for a big increase in Codex usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Zooming out to consider the question of external adoption of coding harnesses, it’s worth remembering that the AI labs I visited in San Francisco are not typical of companies in the wider economy in some ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Selling AI tokens is the business.</span></strong><span> Everyone at these places is incentivized to use AI, learn about it, and get better at it. But this does not apply at companies in other sectors like retail, for example.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No AI spending limits.</span></strong><span> Most companies do not have this luxury, while mid-sized-and-above tech companies are already capping AI usage in engineering. It’s hard to foresee such places doling out unlimited AI tokens to non-engineers!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI labs hire highly autonomous people. </span></strong><span>These places pay up to 50-100% above the top of the market, and attract folks with very high agency, who are extremely open to changing their workflows. Most workplaces are not like this.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So overall, I personally do expect non-engineering orgs to use tools like Codex, Claude Cowork, and similar ones a lot more, but not for them to hit 90%+ adoption within months. Nonetheless, visiting AI labs to learn about how they work is always valuable because I sense they’re months ahead of the rest of the industry in some key regards.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Will the main task of engineers be to make agents more efficient?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While visiting OpenAI, Anthropic, and Cursor, I took the chance to ask engineers how their jobs today are different from the recent past.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Anthropic, Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, told me something interesting: more and more of his work focuses on figuring out ways to make multiple agents “under him” more efficient. For example, he did a massive migration within the last two months that would normally take a year to complete. Instead, he spun up dozens of parallel agents that each took on parts of the migration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>His challenge was to ensure the agents didn’t step on one another’s toes. He did not want to use Git worktrees because he found them too slow. He had all agents work on the same branch and divided the work so they would not touch the same file! Architecting so that agents can work in parallel took a lot of effort, and sounds like interesting, challenging engineering work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This makes me wonder if software engineering could grow into a type of work focused on architecting in order for agents to execute better. </span></strong><span>A day after visiting Anthropic’s offices, I was at Cursor, where I asked the same question of cofounder, Sualeh Asif. He told me that software engineering will increasingly be about building the environment for agents to execute better.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if we look back at the history of software engineering, it has always been about doing the highest-leverage work, while automating away low-leverage things. That’s why compiled languages became so popular because they automated away low-level machine instructions, and also why memory-safe languages became dominant by automating away memory management and errors. Now, we see the automating away of writing code: the next high-leverage work is setting up code architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I cannot speak for the industry, but it was interesting to see how development work is slowly shifting to “architecting the environment of agents” inside of AI labs. Of course, these places are building the platforms that run AI agents, and platform work is rarely the same as product work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Still, as a software engineer, it could be worth experimenting with architecting for agent-type work. </span></strong><span>At the very least, it’s an interesting experiment from which insights can be learned about the constraints of today’s AI agents. Also, this skill could become in-demand in the future, so there’s an opportunity to get hands-on with it now!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Next trend: companies aggressively optimize spend per token?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When talking with engineers, a popular topic was token spend, and token </span><em><span>efficiency,</span></em><span> in particular. Another was GLM-5.2. Let’s start with that:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Is GLM-5.2 the best & cheapest coding model?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GLM-5.2 is a new, open weight, free-to-use model from Chinese lab </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2cfc8161-94b5-4e67-a28b-f42f9641c7a0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>z.AI</span></a><span> which is nearly as capable as Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, as per the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index – as we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e42c8b3-5f60-40c3-b267-9ec199038076?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> two weeks ago. Or is it even better? The code security startup, Semgrep, found this open weight model does much better in cyber benchmarks than Opus 4.8. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8691a841-194e-4ce3-8ee8-951f21fc3479?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>their blog</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We ran a set of popular open-source models against our IDOR benchmark, the same dataset and the same prompt we’ve used to evaluate frontier coding agents. The result surprised us: GLM 5.2, an open-weight model from Zhipu AI, scored a 39% F1 on IDOR detection, beating Claude Code (32%) at roughly $0.17 per vulnerability found. It still trailed Semgrep’s multimodal pipeline (53–61% F1), but that pipeline runs in a purpose-built harness that does a lot of the heavy lifting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Among models given nothing but a prompt, the best open-weight option was no longer the obvious underdog, beating out Claude Opus 4.8</span></strong><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While we were running [this experiment] it we were genuinely shocked. One of the open-weight models, with none of our scaffolding, surpassed a frontier coding agent.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, Anthropic has a more capable model, Fable, but access to that model has been currently blocked by a US government intervention. For cybersecurity use cases reasons, this new Chinese open weight model could be the single best choice for companies without access to Mythos-class models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>GLM-5.2 is getting lots of interest thanks to its cheaper inference, a 1M context window, while offering Opus 4.8-level coding abilities. </span></strong><span>Here’s Maddison Kanna, software engineer at inference provider, Baseten, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dec4156b-49ef-4b0c-a5e4-63ea006daca5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on</span></a><span> what they’re seeing:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Such a vibe shift happening right now. We’ve gotten nonstop requests from people who want to start using GLM-5.2. Incredible few weeks for open source models.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Philip Kiley, also at Baseten, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd77272d-d495-482d-9a58-30e174f74c48?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explains</span></a><span> why GLM-5.2 is such a big deal:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“GLM-5.2 is the biggest news in open models since DeepSeek-R1.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to see why. GLM-5.2 delivers comparable performance to GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 at a fraction of the cost, generally 70-80% less expensive on a pure token basis (use our calculator to estimate savings for your workload).”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>GLM-5.2 was released around when the White House decided to block flagship models from Anthropic and OpenAI for political reasons, </span></strong><span>and</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>the same </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1b158b0d-9f0c-4547-a924-bcefd0d4382e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is now happening</span></a><span> with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6. So, we’re in a situation where Anthropic and OpenAI supposedly have better, more capable models than GLM-5.2, but they are not allowed to release them!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And as it just so happens, at around the same time, Chinese lab Z.ai – an academic spin-off lab founded in 2019 – released a state-of-the-art coding model which is free to use. Of course, “free” here involves paying for inference, but there’s no model licensing fee.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a bit tricky to understand the economics of Z.ai releasing such a capable model for free, when training this model clearly presumably cost an enormous sum. Z.ai is subsidized in part by the Chinese state, so it’s worth asking if these capable open models are China’s attempt to stir up global competition and weaken the business models of rival US companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right now, as long as the US blocks models more advanced than Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 from release, the most capable coding model is an open one from China. It’s predictable that companies everywhere will move their token spend there for cost reasons, if nothing else.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>“Token smart” not “token hard”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cutting back on AI spending is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4397501-8365-4881-a5b5-22a4861fa6d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>turning into</span></a><span> a mega-trend across the industry, as we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4397501-8365-4881-a5b5-22a4861fa6d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> a month ago. But I reckon we could be seeing a new, similarly large trend emerging: tech companies looking to make their token spend more efficient. Coinbase is an example of this. Last week, the company shared that, in the last two months, it cut its spending on tokens by roughly half, while using roughly the same number of tokens as before. Visualizing this:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Coinbase reduced its total token spend by nearly half in the last four months, without greatly reducing usage. Data source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/11ca8a3e-f3dc-49fd-916f-3092d6c2e0b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Coinbase</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Senior staff engineer, Mark Landgrebe, built much of the infra behind these cost savings and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7db5c3c4-872c-4e27-b835-30a1a4adfc47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> the big levers to save cost: routing, caching, and cheaper defaults:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Routing</span></strong><span>: Coinbase routes every LLM request behind its own gateway, which is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/769c5dbf-2a68-4089-89e0-197ad0b5581a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LibreChat</span></a><span>. This LLM gateway has cross-provider failover, so, if one provider does not respond, the prompt is routed to another. It has sensitive data redaction built in, and logging, as well as cost control. It’s like an LLM control plane!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cheaper default models</span></strong><span>: Coinbase is starting to experiment with defaulting to open weight models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7 through its LLM gateway. GLM 5.2 is cheaper to serve than Opus 4.8, while having similar coding efficiency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Caching</span></strong><span>: when running longer tasks like a coding session, it’s a massive waste to send over the full (and growing!) context window to the LLM provider every time. Coinbase improved its routing layer so they went from 5% cache hits to 60%. Now, each request is charged for the </span><em><span>net new </span></em><span>tokens, and not the existing context window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Wipe context when starting a new task: </span></strong><span>when starting a new task, the context is wiped clean, lowering the cost, avoiding “context rot”, and improving the prompt’s efficiency.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>LLM costs are high enough at many companies that optimizing token spend is worthwhile. </span></strong><span>Coinbase employs around 1,000 software engineers, so it makes sense to invest at the infra level in a better routing and caching layer, alongside using the new GLM-5.2 model as the default.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div The agent reads your actual app, writes the integration where it belongs, then typechecks and builds so it can fix errors along the way. AuthKit gives you hosted auth, customizable UI, MFA, social login, session management, and a path to enterprise features like SSO and SCIM when you need them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Free up to 1 million MAUs.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_063026","text":"Try it now →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/36b396ca-4f9f-4376-baaa-efa566d2c8bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Try it now →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>What feels like a real-time conversation with AI today is built from many parts working together.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>At the center sits a language model that works in turns, the same way ChatGPT does when you type to it. The responsiveness comes from a layer of helper systems wrapped around that model, predicting when the user has paused, transcribing audio, generating speech from text, and weaving the pieces together fast enough that the conversation feels fluid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, new research from Thinking Machines argues that this whole approach has a ceiling, and proposes a different way to build AI systems for real-time interaction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines is a relatively new AI research lab focused on human-AI collaboration, publishing research under the name Connectionism and offering developer-facing products for the broader community. What sets them apart is the problem they have identified as central. Most AI labs treat autonomous capability as the most important capability to push forward, meaning the ability for a model to take a task, do the work on its own, and return a result.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines argues this framing sidelines humans. Real work, in their view, benefits from continuous collaboration where the human clarifies, redirects, and gives feedback as the model goes along. The interface should support that, rather than treating the human as someone who hands off a task and walks away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at what the research preview covers and the concept of an interaction model proposed by Thinking Machines.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from the Thinking Machines Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Bottleneck</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The problem starts with how today’s models actually experience the world. A typical language model works in a single thread. It waits for the user to finish typing or speaking before it can perceive any input. Once the model starts generating a response, its perception freezes, and any new input gets queued for later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines compares this setup to resolving a crucial disagreement over email rather than in person. The bandwidth is just too narrow. So much of what makes a collaboration work, the way your voice shifts when uncertain, the moment of realizing a direction change is needed mid-sentence, the reaction on your face when the other person says something useful, all of it gets stripped out of the channel between human and model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This matters because real work that benefits from another mind in the room depends on that bandwidth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A model that only sees clean, finalized inputs forces a person to think like a model, preparing the full request, handing it over, and then waiting. In contrast, real collaboration is often messy, interruptive, and full of mid-stream corrections. Until the interface allows for that, the human ends up doing extra work to fit how the model wants to operate. Thinking Machines argues this bottleneck explains why much of today’s AI work feels like prompting and waiting rather than collaborating the way two people might.</span></p><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Harness</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If today’s voice AI feels real-time despite this limitation, how is that even working to a large extent? The answer is a pattern called a harness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A typical voice AI product is a stack of components glued together:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Voice activity detection listens for pauses and decides when the user has stopped speaking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A speech-to-text model transcribes what was said.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A language model generates a text response.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A text-to-speech model converts that response back into audio.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A dialog manager orchestrates the entire pipeline so the latency feels acceptable.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Imagine a brilliant scholar who communicates only through letters slipped under a door. Making this feel like a conversation requires helpers. One stands outside listening for when the visitor stops talking, another reads the scholar’s letters aloud when they come back, and a third rings a bell when something visible happens that the scholar should know about.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The setup mostly works, but the scholar still experiences reality through letters. Voice tones, facial expressions, the moment itself, all of it stays beyond the scholar’s reach. This is what every real-time voice AI actually is, with a turn-based language model at the center surrounded by helpers that simulate conversation around it.</span></p><div justify"><span>Why does this approach have a ceiling?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It is because the helpers are simpler than the model itself. Voice activity detection runs on raw audio signals using a much smaller and lighter model than the language model behind it. This limits whole categories of behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The system struggles with proactive interjections like “interrupt me when I say something wrong,” because the helper deciding when to speak operates purely on acoustic signals, while correctness remains the language model’s job. Visual reactions like “tell me when I’ve written a bug in my code” face the same problem, because the helper handles audio while anything on screen stays beyond its reach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is where Thinking Machines points to an important lesson. As per a famous essay by Rich Sutton, methods leveraging general computation and learning consistently outperform methods that bake in human-designed heuristics. The same argument led from hand-crafted computer vision features to deep learning, and from hand-crafted game heuristics to self-play. Applied to interactivity, harness components are exactly the kind of hand-crafted heuristic that scale will eventually push out. The way past the ceiling is to put interactivity inside the model itself.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c9122a2-1ebb-4441-a140-8c744fbbcdc4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">How engineering teams resolve incidents in minutes instead of hours. justify"><span>Three design choices stand behind this architecture:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first is time-aligned micro-turns, which change what the model treats as the unit of conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second is an approach that skips heavy pretrained encoders, with audio and video going through lightweight processing components trained from scratch rather than being routed through standalone systems like Whisper.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third is a two-model coordination scheme where a fast interaction model works alongside a slower background model that handles deeper reasoning.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines also did significant work on optimizing inference for this design, including contributing a streaming session feature back to the open-source SGLang library, enabling 200-millisecond chunks to be processed efficiently.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Micro-turns</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Most AI models work in turns, with the user speaking, then the model speaking, then the user speaking again. Each turn is a discrete unit, and the model processes one complete turn at a time. Even when a system handles audio, the underlying logic stays turn-based. The harness simulates real-time, but the model itself perceives the world in clear, separate chunks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines made a different choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Instead of turns, they slice time into 200-millisecond chunks, which they call micro-turns. Every 200 milliseconds, the model takes in whatever arrived across audio, video, and text streams and decides what to output across audio and text streams. Time becomes the fundamental unit, replacing the turn entirely.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure justify"><span>This sounds like a small change, but it transforms what the model can do. The model treats time as continuous rather than partitioned into clean turns, deciding micro-turn by micro-turn whether to speak, listen, jump in, or stay silent. Input and output are happening continuously at the same time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Concretely, this is what unlocks behavior that turn-based systems struggle with.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model can speak while listening, which is how live translation works.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can watch while speaking, which is how live sports commentary works.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can jump in mid-sentence when something visual happens, such as counting pushups in real time as someone exercises.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can also support tasks like “correct my mispronunciation as you hear it,” which requires speaking while listening, something a turn-based architecture handles as separate operations.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These capabilities all share a single source, emerging from the same architectural choice.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Coordination</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Time-aligned micro-turns solve responsiveness, but they create a new problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How does a model designed to respond in 200-millisecond windows also do deep reasoning?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some tasks genuinely require minutes of thinking, web browsing, tool use, or chained reasoning steps. Building a single model that handles both fast response and deep thought at the same time is hard.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines’ answer is to use two models working together:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The interaction model is fast, present, and handles real-time conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The background model is slower and handles sustained reasoning, tool use, browsing, and longer-horizon work.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>They share context with each other, so both have the same picture of what has been said and what is happening.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td justify"><span>`</span><span>The coordination works like this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>When the interaction model encounters something that needs deeper reasoning, it sends a rich context package over to the background model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>This is the full conversation rather than a standalone query, which lets the background model understand the situation fully.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The background model runs asynchronously, with results streaming back as it produces them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The interaction model then weaves those results into the conversation when the moment fits, rather than as an abrupt context switch in the middle of something else.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>From the user’s perspective, this is a single continuous conversation, with one AI thinking, responding, occasionally pausing to dig deeper, and weaving back in smoothly. Behind the scenes, two systems coordinate throughout.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This same logic shows up across computing, with fast paths paired with slow paths, foreground processes paired with background ones, and routine examples throughout operating systems and web browsers. What Thinking Machines did is apply the pattern to AI inference in a principled way, instead of treating reasoning latency as a problem the user has to absorb.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Capabilities</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of these design choices add up. The interaction model handles its own dialog management, knowing whether the user is thinking, yielding, or self-correcting, and it can interject verbally or visually based on context. It can speak and listen at the same time, which is what makes live translation possible. It has a direct sense of elapsed time, and can call tools, search, and generate UI concurrently with the conversation, weaving results back as they become ready.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These claims need evidence. Existing benchmarks for voice AI struggle to capture these qualitative jumps, so Thinking Machines built their own.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>TimeSpeak measures whether the model can initiate speech at user-specified times with the correct content, with an example task being “remind me to breathe in and out every 4 seconds until I ask you to stop.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>CueSpeak measures whether the model speaks at the right moment while the user is still talking, with an example task being “every time I codeswitch, give me the correct word in the original language.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>RepCount-A streams video of someone doing reps after the instruction “count out reps for pushups.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>ProactiveVideoQA streams videos with questions whose correct answers depend on what is happening visually at specific moments.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table
